templates.title: Correctable memory errors per GPU per day, from a counter that resets on reload
templates.subtopic: LAG over cumulative counters, counter resets, daily attribution, top-1 per group

sections.scenario: A GPU cluster operator polls every GPU a few times a day and stores the value of its cumulative correctable memory error counter. Correctable errors are fixed in hardware and do not crash a job, but a GPU whose count climbs quickly is a candidate for a closer look before it starts failing jobs. The counter is cumulative since the driver was last loaded: when the driver is reloaded, it starts again from 0, and each reading carries the driver_load_id it was read under. The reliability team wants a daily list of nodes with GPUs whose counter increased by at least {{threshold}} in a day.
sections.problem:
Table gpu_error_samples(sample_id, node_id, gpu_uuid, sample_ts, driver_load_id, ce_total) holds {{samples}} readings from {{gpus}} GPUs. Write one PostgreSQL query that returns day, node_id, flagged_gpus, worst_gpu, worst_increase.

For each GPU, order its readings by sample_ts and compare each reading with the previous one:

  • if both were read under the same driver_load_id, the increase is ce_total − previous ce_total;
  • if driver_load_id changed, the driver was reloaded in between and the counter restarted from 0, so the increase is the new ce_total itself;
  • a GPU's first reading has no increase.

An increase belongs to the UTC date of the later reading. A GPU's daily increase is the sum of its increases on that date, and a GPU is flagged on a day when its daily increase is at least {{threshold}}. Return one row per (day, node) with at least {{min_gpus}} flagged GPUs: how many GPUs on the node were flagged, the flagged GPU with the largest daily increase (ties to the smaller gpu_uuid) and that increase. Order by day, node_id. {{null_rule}} {{reset_rule}}
sections.constraints: One SQL statement (CTEs allowed). A GPU stays on its node for the whole sample. Two readings of the same GPU never share a sample_ts.
sections.assumptions: The counter's behaviour (cumulative since driver load, restarting from 0 on reload), the polling schedule and the threshold are this exercise's hypothetical model, not the specification of any product; check current docs for how a given driver exposes its error counters. Uncorrectable errors and driver error events are out of scope here.
sections.criteria: Readings ordered by time per GPU; failed reads removed before neighbours are paired (Hard+); a reset recognised by a change of driver_load_id and its increase taken as the new value (Very Hard: including a reset with no drop); the first reading excluded; increases dated by the later reading in UTC; inclusive threshold; minimum flagged GPUs per node-day; worst GPU with the stated tie-break; deterministic order; can discuss incremental computation and how to validate a drain signal.

clarifications.q: Why not just take the largest reading of the day minus the smallest?
clarifications.a: A reload in the middle of the day restarts the counter, so max − min mixes two different counts and can even go negative.

clarifications.q: The previous reading is on the day before. Which day gets the increase?
clarifications.a: The later reading's UTC date. The errors were observed by the reading that reported them.

clarifications.q: Is the threshold inclusive?
clarifications.a: Yes. A daily increase exactly equal to {{threshold}} is flagged.

clarifications.q: A reload happened and the new value is higher than the old one. Is that a reset?
clarifications.a: Yes. A reset is any change of driver_load_id; the value alone does not tell you.

clarifications.q: Can the same GPU appear on two nodes?
clarifications.a: Not in this sample.

hints: LAG(ce_total) and LAG(driver_load_id) over PARTITION BY gpu_uuid ORDER BY sample_ts give each reading its predecessor.
Decide what a row means before you aggregate: one row per reading with its increase and its day.
Filter rows you should not compare before the window, not after it: a window computed over rows you later discard pairs the wrong neighbours.
ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY day, node_id ORDER BY increase DESC, gpu_uuid) together with COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY day, node_id) gives the worst GPU and the count in one pass.
followups: Readings arrive a few hours apart. How would you attribute an increase that spans midnight more fairly, and is that worth the complexity?
The fleet grows to hundreds of thousands of GPUs polled every minute. How would you compute daily increases incrementally, without re-reading the whole history each day?
A node's GPUs all jump at the same moment. What could explain that besides failing memory, and how would you tell the cases apart in data?
How would you turn this daily list into a drain decision with a measured false-positive rate?

rules.ask: A GPU's driver was reloaded at noon. What does max minus min of the day's readings give you, and is it the number of errors?
Some reads failed and stored NULL. Where in your query do they disappear, before or after the window, and why does that matter?
Is sample_id guaranteed to follow time? What happens to your increases if it does not?
After a reload the counter can climb past its old value before the next reading. Does your reset test still see it?
Which reading's date does an increase spanning midnight belong to in your query, and why?

templates.title: Work lost to restarts: steps recomputed after each restore, and the GPU-hours they cost
templates.subtopic: sessionising event streams into runs, latest-before lookup, GROUPING SETS, ratio of totals

sections.scenario: A team running long training jobs on a shared GPU cluster saves checkpoints every few hundred steps. When a run is interrupted, the job restarts from its last saved checkpoint, so every step since that checkpoint is computed twice. The platform team wants to show each team how much of its GPU time went into recomputing work, to decide whether more frequent checkpoints would pay for themselves.
sections.problem:
Tables jobs(job_id, team) ({{jobs}} jobs) and job_events(event_id, job_id, event_ts, event_type, step, gpus) ({{events}} events). {{types_rule}} A job's events, in event_ts order, form runs: a run begins with a start event (its step is the step training resumes from, its gpus the GPUs the run holds) and ends with the next fail, preempt or complete event, whose step is the step reached. A checkpoint event inside a run saved that run's state at its step. {{gpus_rule}}

When a run is interrupted (it ends with fail or preempt), its restore point is the latest checkpoint of that run at or before the interruption (a checkpoint in the same second as the interruption counts), or the run's own start if the run saved none. For each interruption:

  • recomputed steps = interruption step − restore point step;
  • lost GPU-seconds = seconds from the restore point's event_ts to the interruption × the run's gpus.

A job's total GPU-seconds is the sum over all its runs of the run's duration in seconds × its gpus.

Write one PostgreSQL query returning team, job_id, interruptions, recomputed_steps, lost_gpu_hours, lost_share: one row per job (every job, including jobs never interrupted), and after each team's jobs one team row with job_id NULL that sums the team's jobs. lost_gpu_hours = lost GPU-seconds / 3600 rounded to 2 places; lost_share = lost GPU-seconds / total GPU-seconds rounded to 4 places (for the team row, of the team's totals). Order by team, then job_id with the team row last.
sections.constraints: One SQL statement (CTEs allowed). Every run ends before the next start of its job, and every job's last run is complete. event_id is assigned at load time and is not in time order.
sections.assumptions: Jobs, teams, step rates, checkpoint intervals and GPU counts are hypothetical. The model is deliberately simple: a restart resumes exactly from the restore point, step time is constant, and the time spent loading a checkpoint is ignored.
sections.criteria: Runs reconstructed per job in time order; the restore point is the latest checkpoint in the run at or before the interruption, else the start; preemptions counted like failures (Hard+); failed checkpoint attempts ignored and each run charged at its own GPU count (Very Hard); never-interrupted jobs present with zeros and counted in team totals; team shares as ratios of totals; correct rounding from unrounded seconds; NULL job_id for team rows and the stated order; can reason about checkpoint intervals and streaming computation.

clarifications.q: A checkpoint and a failure have the same event_ts. Was the checkpoint saved?
clarifications.a: Yes. A checkpoint at the same second as the interruption counts; nothing after it was lost.

clarifications.q: Can a run restore from a checkpoint saved in an earlier run?
clarifications.a: Not directly: the run's start step is already that checkpoint. If the run saved none of its own, its restore point is its start.

clarifications.q: Does the time between an interruption and the next start count as GPU time?
clarifications.a: No. Only time inside runs is counted, in both the lost and the total GPU-seconds.

clarifications.q: For the team row, is the share the average of the jobs' shares?
clarifications.a: No. It is the team's lost GPU-seconds over the team's total GPU-seconds.

clarifications.q: Which GPU count applies to a run?
clarifications.a: The gpus on that run's start event.

hints: Number the runs: a running count of start events per job, ordered by event_ts, gives every event its run.
One row per run with FILTERed aggregates: start time and step, GPUs, end time and step, how it ended, and its latest checkpoint.
GREATEST(start, latest checkpoint) is the restore point; a run with no checkpoint has a NULL latest checkpoint, so COALESCE first.
GROUP BY GROUPING SETS ((team, job_id), (team)) produces both the job rows and the team rows; compute shares from summed seconds, not from rounded hours.
followups: Given a team's failure rate and the time a checkpoint takes to save, how would you choose the checkpoint interval that minimises expected lost plus checkpointing time?
Preemptions are announced a short time in advance. How would you measure how much lost work a checkpoint-on-preempt policy would have saved, from this data?
Runs restart on a different number of GPUs and the step rate changes. Which of your measures still mean the same thing?
Events come from thousands of jobs as a stream, sometimes late. How would you compute these numbers continuously?

rules.ask: Your LAG looks one event back. What if a failed checkpoint attempt or another event sits between the checkpoint and the interruption?
How does your team row's share come out: from summed seconds, or from the rounded job values? Show where the difference would appear.
Is the team's share the average of its jobs' shares? What happens when one small job lost half its time and a large one lost almost none?
Is event_id in time order here? What breaks if you number runs by it?
A checkpoint and the interruption share a second. Which restore point does your query pick, and what does the rule say?

templates.title: Queue wait by request size: median minutes to start per partition and GPU bucket
templates.subtopic: range join to a bucket table, PERCENTILE_CONT medians, conditional counts, HAVING floors

sections.scenario: A GPU cluster operator runs a batch scheduler with several partitions. Users keep asking "if I ask for more GPUs, how much longer will I wait?" The operator wants a table of typical queue waits by partition and by how many GPUs a job requested, using the median because a few jobs that wait for hours would drag an average far from what most users see.
sections.problem:
Table job_attempts(job_id, attempt, partition_name, gpus_requested, queued_at, started_at, cancelled_at) has {{rows}} rows; gpu_buckets(bucket_min, bucket_max, label) defines the buckets {{buckets}} (a NULL bucket_max means no upper bound; both bounds are inclusive). {{attempt_rule}}

A job's queue wait is from its attempt 1 queued_at to its attempt 1 started_at, in minutes. A job whose attempt 1 has no started_at but has a cancelled_at was cancelled before start: it has no wait and is counted separately. {{cancel_rule}}

Write one PostgreSQL query returning partition_name, bucket_min, gpu_bucket, jobs_started, cancelled_before_start, median_wait_min: one row per partition and bucket (by gpus_requested), where jobs_started is the number of jobs that started, cancelled_before_start the number cancelled before start, and median_wait_min the median queue wait (PERCENTILE_CONT(0.5), so with an even count the mean of the two middle waits) rounded to 2 places. Leave out groups with fewer than {{min_jobs}} started jobs. Order by partition_name, bucket_min.
sections.constraints: One SQL statement (CTEs allowed). (job_id, attempt) is unique; a job keeps its partition and GPU request across attempts. Every gpus_requested falls in exactly one bucket.
sections.assumptions: Partitions, bucket boundaries, waits and the floor are hypothetical, and the scheduler is a generic batch scheduler, not any particular product. A median of waits that ended ignores jobs still waiting, which biases it low when the queue is long; the follow-ups return to that.
sections.criteria: Range join with inclusive bounds and an open-ended top bucket; attempt 1 only (Very Hard); cancelled-before-start excluded from the median and counted separately; jobs cancelled after starting kept and still-waiting jobs left out (Hard+); PERCENTILE_CONT median with numeric rounding; floor on started jobs inclusive; deterministic order by bucket lower bound; can discuss censoring, forecasting and approximate quantiles.

clarifications.q: Do cancelled jobs count in jobs_started?
clarifications.a: A job cancelled before it started does not; it is counted in cancelled_before_start. A job cancelled after it started did start, so it counts.

clarifications.q: Does the floor count cancelled jobs?
clarifications.a: No. The floor is on jobs_started.

clarifications.q: A job asks for exactly the upper bound of a bucket. Where does it go?
clarifications.a: In that bucket: both bounds are inclusive.

clarifications.q: How is the median computed with an even number of jobs?
clarifications.a: PERCENTILE_CONT(0.5): the mean of the two middle waits.

clarifications.q: Should a job that was requeued contribute two waits?
clarifications.a: No. This report is about the first wait from submission to start; attempt 1 only.

hints: Join to the bucket table with a range condition, and decide what happens when bucket_max is NULL before you write BETWEEN.
PERCENTILE_CONT(0.5) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY …) ignores NULL values, so jobs that never started fall out of the median on their own.
COUNT(started_at) counts non-NULL values; COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE …) counts any condition.
PERCENTILE_CONT returns double precision; cast to numeric before ROUND(…, 2).
followups: Jobs still waiting are left out, so a long queue makes the median look better than it is. How would you report a median that accounts for them?
Users want a forecast for a job they are about to submit. What would you add to this table, and how would you tell them how uncertain it is?
At millions of jobs a day, exact medians per group are expensive. What would you use instead, and what error would you accept?
Large requests wait longer partly because the scheduler holds GPUs back to fit them. How would you separate waiting for capacity from waiting for priority?

rules.ask: A few jobs waited four hours and most waited two minutes. What does the average tell a user, and why did the team ask for a median?
The top bucket has no upper bound. What does BETWEEN bucket_min AND bucket_max do with a NULL bucket_max?
With four jobs in a group, which value does PERCENTILE_DISC return, and what does the question ask for?
A job was cancelled an hour after it started. Is it excluded by your filter, and should it be?
A job was preempted and requeued. Which two timestamps define its wait in your query?

templates.title: Placing GPU slices: first fit on aligned slot boundaries across thousands of GPUs
templates.subtopic: first-fit allocation with lazy invalidation, aligned buddy-style blocks

sections.scenario: A GPU cluster operator partitions GPUs into fixed-size slices so that small inference and notebook workloads can share a GPU. In this exercise's hypothetical layout, each GPU has slots equal slots (4 or 8), and a slice of 1, 2 or 4 slots must start on a slot index that is a multiple of its size, like aligned blocks in a buddy allocator. Before changing the placement policy, the operator wants an exact replay of a day of requests and releases under the current policy: first fit. {{drain_rule}}
sections.problem:
Implement place_slices(num_gpus, slots, ops). GPUs are numbered 0 … num_gpus − 1 and start empty. Process ops in order:

  • ('alloc', req_id, size): place a slice of size slots on the lowest-numbered eligible GPU that has size free slots starting at an offset that is a multiple of size; on that GPU, use the lowest such offset. If no GPU can take it, the request is rejected.
  • ('free', req_id): release that request's slots. {{release_rule}}
  • ('drain', gpu) / ('undrain', gpu): see the scenario.

Return a list with one entry per alloc, in order: (gpu, offset), or None if the request was rejected. A rejected request holds nothing, so a later free of its id does nothing.
sections.constraints: Up to 3 000 GPUs and 150 000 operations, on a cluster that stays nearly full, so free slots left by releases are scattered everywhere. size is 1, 2 or 4 and never larger than slots; request ids are never reused. Expected: about O(log G) per operation. Scanning the GPUs from 0 for every request is too slow.
sections.assumptions: The slot layout, alignment rule and policy are this exercise's own hypothetical model of GPU partitioning; check current docs for how any real partitioning feature lays out its slices, which differ by product. Placement ignores memory, topology and fairness.
sections.criteria: Correct aligned offsets and lowest offset within a GPU; strict first fit across GPUs, including GPUs that become eligible again after a release; rejected requests return None and hold nothing; stale or unknown releases ignored (Hard+); drained GPUs keep their slices and take nothing new until undrained (Very Hard); per-size heaps (or an equivalent ordered structure) with lazy invalidation, O(log G) per operation; can compare first fit and best fit and reason about fragmentation.

clarifications.q: A GPU with 8 slots has slot 1 free and slots 2–3 free. Where does a 2-slot slice go?
clarifications.a: At offset 2. Offsets must be multiples of the size, so slots 1–2 are not a valid 2-slot slice.

clarifications.q: Is "first fit" the first GPU after the last placement (next fit)?
clarifications.a: No. Always the lowest-numbered GPU that can take it, even if it was full a moment ago.

clarifications.q: What should free do with an id that is not currently placed?
clarifications.a: Nothing. It may have been rejected, released already or never seen.

clarifications.q: Should I move slices around to make room (defragment)?
clarifications.a: No. Slices never move.

clarifications.q: Does a rejected request wait and retry?
clarifications.a: No. It is rejected and reported as None.

hints: Represent each GPU as a bitmask of used slots; a slice of size k at offset o is the mask ((1 << k) − 1) << o.
Whether a GPU can take a size-k slice depends only on its mask: at most 8 checks.
For each size keep a min-heap of GPUs that may be able to take it. When the top cannot (anymore), pop it; that check is cheap and each push is paid for by a state change.
A release (and, if present, an undrain) is the only event that makes a GPU eligible again: push it back into the heaps it now fits, unless it is already there.
followups: First fit packs low-numbered GPUs and leaves fragments everywhere else. Construct a small sequence where best fit (the GPU with the fewest free slots that still fits) rejects fewer requests, and one where it rejects more.
Requests now say "any size from 2 to 4, larger preferred". What changes in your data structures?
The operator wants to reconfigure a GPU to a different slot layout, which requires it to be empty. How would you choose which GPUs to drain, and what does this replay tell you about the cost?
Placement must also respect which GPUs share a fast interconnect for multi-slice jobs. How would you extend the heap-per-size idea, and what breaks?

rules.ask: The cluster is nearly full and the free slots are on GPU 2 900. How many GPUs does your loop look at for one request, and for 150 000?
When does a GPU enter a size's heap, and what stops it from being pushed twice?
GPU 0 just released a slice. Does your cursor ever go back to it, and does the specification require that?
A tree over GPUs answers "lowest GPU that fits size k" too. How would you store the per-size answer in each node, and is it worth it over three heaps?
Sorted lists give O(n) inserts in plain Python. How many inserts does the timing test make, and what is your actual cost?

templates.title: Profiler self time: exclusive time per annotated range from nested push/pop events
templates.subtopic: nested intervals per thread, exclusive versus inclusive time, recursion, truncated traces

sections.scenario: A team running training jobs on GPUs annotates its code with named ranges (forward, attention, allreduce, optimizer_step …) so a profiler can show where a step's time goes. Each annotation is recorded as a push when the range opens and a pop when it closes, on the CPU thread that issued it. The total (inclusive) time of forward includes everything inside it, so the team's report needs self time: the time a range spent outside its own child ranges, summed per name. {{thread_rule}}
sections.problem: Implement self_times(events, end_ts). events is the trace in order: ('push', thread, ts, name) opens a range, ('pop', thread, ts) closes the innermost open range of that thread. Ranges on one thread nest like a stack; threads are independent. A range's duration is close time − open time, and its self time is its duration minus the durations of its direct children (ranges opened and closed while it was the innermost open range of the thread). Return {name: (calls, self_time)} with one entry per name that was pushed: how many ranges of that name were opened, and the sum of their self times. {{ragged_rule}}
sections.constraints: Up to 300 000 events, nesting up to 400 deep. Timestamps are integers (nanoseconds) and never decrease along the list; end_ts is at least the last timestamp. Expected: O(n). Finding each range's children by scanning the events it encloses is O(n × depth) and too slow here.
sections.assumptions: The event format is a generic model of annotated-range profiling with integer timestamps, not the output format of any particular profiler; check the current docs of the tool you use for its exact semantics. Asynchronous GPU work launched inside a range is out of scope: this trace measures the CPU-side ranges only.
sections.criteria: One stack per thread; self time = duration − direct children's durations, with a running children total per open range; each instance of a recursive name counted once; list order for equal timestamps; interleaved threads kept apart (Hard+); pops with nothing open ignored and open ranges closed at end_ts, innermost first (Very Hard); O(n) time and O(depth) extra memory per thread; can discuss inclusive time with recursion and asynchronous GPU work.

clarifications.q: Is a grandchild's time subtracted from its grandparent?
clarifications.a: No. Only direct children are subtracted; the grandchild's time is already inside the child's duration.

clarifications.q: A range named matmul opens inside another matmul. Is that one call or two?
clarifications.a: Two calls. Each instance has its own self time, and the sum never counts the same nanosecond twice.

clarifications.q: Two events have the same timestamp. Which happened first?
clarifications.a: The one earlier in the list.

clarifications.q: Can a pop on one thread close a range on another thread?
clarifications.a: No. Each thread has its own stack.

clarifications.q: Can self time be negative?
clarifications.a: Not with a valid trace: children fit inside their parent.

hints: Keep one stack per thread, and for each open range remember its name, start time and the total duration of its children so far.
When a range closes, its self time is its duration minus that children total; then add its duration to the children total of the new top of the stack.
There is no need to build the whole tree or store every range.
If a trace can end with ranges still open, close them from the innermost outwards so their parents receive their durations.
followups: The report also needs inclusive time per name. With recursion (a name inside itself), how do you avoid counting the same time twice?
Two runs of the same model are traced. How would you compare them range by range, when names repeat thousands of times per step?
GPU kernels launched inside a range run later and asynchronously. How would you attribute kernel time back to the ranges that launched them?
The trace is 50 GB across many processes. How would you compute self times in a distributed job, given that a range can span chunk boundaries?

rules.ask: A range at depth 1 encloses 300 000 events. How many events does your inner loop look at in total for the whole trace?
Inclusive time of matmul when matmul nests inside itself: which instances' durations do you add, and why?
Do you need the tree at all? What is the least you must keep per open range to get self time when it closes?
The events are already in time order per thread. What does sorting cost you, and what does it lose when timestamps are equal?
Thread 2 pops while thread 1 has a range open. Which range does your stack close?

templates.title: A caching allocator for GPU memory: best fit, split and coalesce
templates.subtopic: memory allocation, best fit, splitting, coalescing, fragmentation

sections.scenario: Asking the GPU driver for memory is slow, so deep-learning frameworks commonly put a caching allocator in front of it. The allocator reserves large segments from the device, hands out blocks carved from them, and keeps freed blocks in a cache to reuse, never giving memory back unless asked. A training team sees jobs fail with out-of-memory errors while the dashboard shows gigabytes "free". They have recorded the allocation trace of one training step and want to replay it through a model of the allocator, to see how much memory is reserved at the peak and how fragmented the cache is. {{trace_rule}}
sections.problem:
Implement simulate_allocator(events, segment_bytes, min_split). events is a list, in order, of ("alloc", id, nbytes), ("free", id) and ("empty_cache",). Addresses are integers.

  1. Rounding. A request for nbytes (at least 1) needs need bytes: nbytes rounded up to a multiple of 512.
  2. Best fit. Among cached free blocks of at least need bytes, take the smallest; if two are the same size, the one at the lower address.
  3. New segment. If no cached block fits, reserve a new segment of need rounded up to a multiple of segment_bytes. The first segment starts at address 0, and each new segment starts where the previous new segment ended, so addresses are never reused, even after a segment is released. The new segment is one free block, and the request is served from it.
  4. Split. The allocation takes the start of the chosen block. If the block's size minus need is at least min_split, the rest becomes a cached free block right after it. Otherwise the allocation keeps the whole block.
  5. Free. Freeing a live id returns its block to the cache and merges it with the free block that ends where it starts and the free block that starts where it ends, but only within the same segment. A free for an id that is not live changes nothing.
  6. empty_cache. Every segment that is now a single free block is released.

Return a dict: "addresses", the address each alloc received, in event order; "peak_reserved", the most bytes reserved at any moment; and, after the last event, "reserved" (bytes in segments not released), "allocated" (total size of the blocks held by live ids, including any slack kept by rule 4), "free_blocks" (number of cached free blocks) and "largest_free" (size of the largest one, or 0).
sections.constraints: Up to 150 000 events, with thousands of free blocks cached at once. segment_bytes and min_split are positive multiples of 512. Ids of live allocations are unique. Expected: O(log F) to find a block among F cached blocks, plus the cost of keeping them in order. Scanning every cached block for each request is too slow.
sections.assumptions: The rounding size, segment sizes and split rule are this exercise's rules, a simplified model of how caching allocators commonly behave; check a real framework's documentation for its own. There is one device, one stream and no limit on device memory.
sections.criteria: Correct rounding, best fit with the lower address on ties, splitting only when the remainder reaches min_split, merging on both sides without crossing segments, segment addresses never reused, empty_cache releasing only fully free segments, ignored double frees, and every counter exact; a sorted structure with binary search and O(1) neighbour lookups; a clear complexity argument; sensible answers about fragmentation, pools and streams.

clarifications.q: Two free blocks have the same size. Which one do I use?
clarifications.a: The one at the lower address, regardless of which was freed more recently.

clarifications.q: Two segments sit next to each other in the address space and are both completely free. Do they merge?
clarifications.a: No. Blocks only merge within one segment.

clarifications.q: After empty_cache releases a segment, does the next segment reuse its addresses?
clarifications.a: No. New segments always start at the highest address reserved so far.

clarifications.q: Does allocated count the bytes asked for or the block size?
clarifications.a: The block size, which includes the rounding and any remainder kept by the split rule.

clarifications.q: Is a free block left over when a request uses a whole new segment?
clarifications.a: Only if the remainder is at least min_split.

hints: Keep the free blocks in a list sorted by (size, address). bisect_left(blocks, (need, -1)) lands on the best fit.
To merge, you need the free block that starts at an address and the free block that ends at an address. Two dicts answer both in O(1).
Store each block's segment bounds with it, so that a merge can check it stays inside the segment.
followups: The peak reserved bytes are 30% above the peak allocated bytes. Using your replay, how would you tell whether that is fragmentation or a short burst, and what would you change in the allocator's policy?
Real allocators keep separate pools for small and large blocks and round large requests more coarsely. What problem does each of those solve, and what does it cost?
Two CUDA streams use the same allocator. Why can a block freed by one stream not be reused immediately by the other, and how would you model that in the replay?
The team wants the replay to explain each out-of-memory error. What would you record per event so that a report can say which blocks were in the way?

rules.ask: Show a trace where first fit and best fit give different addresses. Which one leaves the larger free block behind, and does that always help?
insort on a Python list moves elements. What is the real cost per insertion with 5 000 cached blocks, and when would you reach for a balanced tree or a heap of per-size buckets?
A heap gives you the smallest block, but best fit needs the smallest block at least need bytes. How do you get that from a heap, and what does a free in the middle cost?
Two adjacent segments are both empty. What stops your code merging them, and why does that rule exist in a real allocator?
Releasing memory to the driver lowers reserved. Why would a framework avoid doing that in every step, and what does it cost the next step?

templates.title: Where did the step time change? One exact split of a training run
templates.subtopic: change-point detection, least squares, integer comparison

sections.scenario: A team running training jobs on GPUs records the wall-clock time of every training step. When a job slows down, for example after a node is swapped, a library upgrade or a change in data loading, the first question is when it changed. A simple and well-understood answer is the single split of the step-time series into "before" and "after" that best explains the data with two constant levels, reported only when it explains enough to be worth an alert. The alert runs on every job, and its answer must not depend on floating-point luck. {{data_rule}}
sections.problem:
Implement find_change_point(step_ns, min_len, max_ratio_pct). step_ns lists one job's step times in step order, as integer nanoseconds. A split k puts steps 0 … k−1 before and k … n−1 after, and is allowed only if both parts have at least min_len steps. The cost of a part is its sum of squared differences from its own mean (its SSE); the cost of a split is the cost of the part before plus the cost of the part after.

  1. Choose the allowed split with the lowest cost. If two splits cost exactly the same, choose the smaller k.
  2. Report it only if the original series has a cost above 0 and the split's cost is at most max_ratio_pct percent of the original series' cost (split_cost × 100 ≤ max_ratio_pct × series_cost, exactly).
  3. Return (k, mean_before, mean_after) with the two means as floats. Return None if no split is allowed (n < 2 × min_len), if the series is constant, or if the best split fails rule 2.
sections.constraints: Up to 200 000 steps; values up to 10 000 000 000. min_len ≥ 1; 0 ≤ max_ratio_pct ≤ 100. Comparisons in rules 1 and 2 must be exact: two splits whose costs are equal as rational numbers are a tie. Expected O(n). Recomputing both parts' costs for every split is O(n²) and too slow.
sections.assumptions: Step times and thresholds are hypothetical. One split is enough here; jobs with several changes are a follow-up. The cost is the classic least-squares criterion for one change in the mean.
sections.criteria: Correct split with the smaller k on exact ties; min_len respected; None for too-short series, constant series and splits that explain too little, with an inclusive boundary; running sums giving O(n); exact integer comparisons by cross-multiplication; means returned correctly; clear reasoning about outliers, several changes and incremental updates.

clarifications.q: Can I use floats?
clarifications.a: For the returned means, yes. The choice of k and the threshold test must be exact; with values near 10¹⁰, sums of squares reach 10²⁰ and more, beyond what a float holds exactly.

clarifications.q: Two splits have exactly the same cost. Which do I return?
clarifications.a: The smaller k.

clarifications.q: What if the series is constant?
clarifications.a: None: there is nothing to explain.

clarifications.q: Is the boundary in rule 2 inclusive?
clarifications.a: Yes. A split costing exactly max_ratio_pct percent of the original is reported.

clarifications.q: What does min_len protect against?
clarifications.a: Splits that only isolate the first few warm-up steps or a single outlier. Splits closer than min_len to either end are not allowed.

hints: The SSE of a part with m values, sum s and sum of squares q is q − s²/m. Running sums give s and q for every prefix in O(1).
The total sum of squares is the same for every split, so minimising the cost means maximising L²/k + R²/(n−k), where L and R are the sums of the two parts.
Compare a/b with c/d as a·d with c·b (all positive). Python integers do not overflow.
followups: Your alert fires on a job whose step time rises slowly over a day. Is a single change in the mean the right model, and what would you report instead?
A job has two changes: a node swap and, later, a data-loader fix. How would you extend this to find several change points, and what stops it from splitting the noise?
Checkpoint saves make one step in a thousand take ten times as long. What do they do to the squared-error cost, and what more robust cost would you use?
The detector runs every minute on a growing series for 20 000 jobs. How do you avoid recomputing from step 0 each time, and what exactly do you keep per job?

rules.ask: With step times near 10¹⁰ ns, how many exact digits does a float keep in a sum of squares? Show how two exactly equal costs could compare unequal.
Fractions are exact. What do they cost per split at 200 000 steps, and how would you get the same exactness with plain integers?
What is the total work when you recompute the sums for every split, and what can you carry from split k to split k + 1?
A rolling-mean rule fires when the slowdown is already old. How would you get the step where it started, and how confident are you in it?

templates.title: Debug the GPU utilisation rollup
templates.subtopic: fractional slices, preemption, day boundaries, missing data, per-GPU lookups

sections.scenario: A GPU cluster operator charges each team for the GPU-hours it holds and reports how busy those GPUs were, from utilisation samples taken on every GPU. Some GPUs are partitioned into fixed-size slices, so a job can hold part of a GPU. The daily report has drawn complaints. Teams that run on slices show no usage at all. One team was charged for four hours on a job that was preempted after one. Teams with long overnight runs see nothing on the second day. Teams on newer nodes, where GPUs of two models share a node, are charged wrong amounts. And a node whose telemetry agent restarted shows those teams' GPUs as nearly idle. The rollup below is the suspect. {{replay_rule}}
sections.problem:
Fix utilisation_rollup(allocations, samples, inventory, slots_per_gpu, interval) so that it meets this specification.

  1. Inputs. allocations is a list of dicts {"job", "team", "node", "gpu", "slots", "start", "end"}, with an optional "preempted_at". gpu is the GPU's index on its node. inventory[node] lists the GPU model at each index; one node can hold several models. slots_per_gpu[model] is how many slices a GPU of that model is split into. samples is a list of (node, gpu, ts, util): the GPU's utilisation in percent over the interval seconds starting at ts. Times are Unix seconds, UTC.
  2. Share. An allocation holds slots / slots_per_gpu[model] of a GPU, where model is that GPU's own model.
  3. Held time. An allocation holds its share from start until preempted_at if it is present, otherwise until end.
  4. GPU-hours. A team is charged share × held seconds / 3600, split at each midnight UTC and charged to the day each part falls on.
  5. Utilisation. A sample belongs to every allocation holding that GPU at ts (start ≤ ts < stop), on the UTC day of ts. A team's average utilisation for a day is Σ(util × share × interval) / Σ(share × interval) over the samples that belong to its allocations that day. A missing sample is unknown: it counts in neither sum. With no samples, the average is None.
  6. Output. {(day, team): (gpu_hours, avg_util)} for every day and team charged more than 0, day as "YYYY-MM-DD", both numbers rounded to 3 decimals.
sections.constraints: Keep the function's shape and output format. About 250 000 samples and a few thousand allocations, in a few seconds. The slices held at once on one GPU never exceed its slot count.
sections.assumptions: Models, slot counts, teams and samples are hypothetical. Attributing a whole-GPU utilisation sample to every slice on that GPU is this exercise's simplification; real partitioned GPUs can report per-slice metrics.
sections.criteria: Finds and explains every bug with its business symptom; the model looked up per GPU; fractional shares; preempted allocations end at preempted_at for both charging and sample attribution; GPU-hours split at midnight UTC; missing samples excluded from the average, None with no samples; a minimal fix that keeps the output; a test per bug.

clarifications.q: Two teams hold slices of one GPU at the same time. Who gets the sample?
clarifications.a: Both, each weighted by its own share.

clarifications.q: A sample's timestamp equals an allocation's end. Does it belong to it?
clarifications.a: No. The held interval is start ≤ ts < stop; the sample belongs to the next holder, if any.

clarifications.q: Should a missing sample count as 0 % utilisation?
clarifications.a: No. It is unknown, so it is left out of both the numerator and the denominator.

clarifications.q: Which day does a sample belong to?
clarifications.a: The UTC day of its ts.

clarifications.q: How many bugs are there?
clarifications.a: Several, of different kinds. Each has a test named after it.

hints: Find a node whose GPUs are not all the same model and check which model the code looks up for GPU 2.
Evaluate 3 // 7 and 3 / 7 in Python.
Look for every place that uses a["end"].
An allocation runs from 22:00 to 02:00 UTC. Which days does the code charge, and how much?
Write the average for an hour with 60 samples expected and 55 present, both ways.
followups: Write the smallest set of unit tests that would have caught every one of these bugs.
Samples arrive late from nodes whose clocks drift. Which days' results can change after they are published, and how would you restate them?
Finance wants GPU-hours by team for a month to match the scheduler's own accounting exactly. Where can the two disagree, and which one should be the source of truth?
At 100 000 GPUs with one sample per second, the inner loop over allocations per GPU is the cost. How would you join samples to allocations in a warehouse or a stream processor instead?

rules.ask: Your fix looks the model up per GPU. Where else in a cluster's data can a per-node assumption hide, and how would you test for it?
GPU-hours are now fractional. Where do you round, and what does rounding each allocation before summing do to a month's bill?
The finance team's day starts at midnight in their own time zone. What changes in your code, and in what you store?
A node sent no samples for six hours. Should the report show an average, or say how much of the day was observed? What would you add to the output?
A preempted job is restarted on another node. How would you report the GPU-hours lost to preemption per team?

templates.title: Joining per-second GPU samples to the job that held each GPU
templates.subtopic: interval joins, downsampling, retention tiers, clock skew

sections.scenario: A GPU cluster operator runs {{gpus}} GPUs. An agent on every node samples {{metrics}} metrics per GPU once a second: utilisation, memory used, power, temperature, clock speeds and error counters. The scheduler records which job, and which slice of a GPU, held each GPU and when. Today the samples sit in a time-series store that knows nothing about jobs. Users want to see their job's GPUs on a dashboard; capacity planners want a year of history by team and GPU model; and engineers investigating a failure want the raw seconds around it. Node clocks are synchronised, but the operator has seen drift of {{clock_skew}} before a node is fixed.
sections.problem: Design the pipeline that joins every sample to the job (and slice) that held that GPU at that second, and serves it at several resolutions. Cover how samples and scheduler events land, the join itself (an interval join keyed by GPU), what happens to samples for a GPU no job held, downsampling (which aggregates you keep per minute and per hour), retention tiers (raw seconds for {{raw_retention}}, then rollups), late and out-of-order samples, node clock skew, and how a dashboard and a capacity report each read the data.
sections.constraints: Raw seconds must stay queryable for {{raw_retention}}. Rollups must be reproducible: rebuilding an hour gives the same numbers. Scheduler events (allocate, release, preempt) can arrive minutes after the samples they explain. A job's dashboard should lag real time by less than a minute.
sections.assumptions: All volumes, metrics and retention periods are hypothetical. Each sample carries a node id, a GPU index, the node's own timestamp and the values. Each scheduler event carries a job id, a node, a GPU index, a slice, an event type and the scheduler's timestamp. You may use common building blocks: a partitioned log, a stream processor, object storage with a columnar format, a time-series database, a warehouse.
sections.criteria: A holding-interval table derived from scheduler events, with open intervals and corrections; an interval join per GPU that handles slices; idle samples kept and labelled; mergeable rollup aggregates (sum, count, min, max, sketches, counter deltas); explicit lateness and clock-skew handling with a correction path; retention tiers sized and justified; reproducible rollups by partition rebuild; serving paths for the dashboard and for long-range reports; a plan for each incident.

clarifications.q: Is the GPU or the job the main key?
clarifications.a: Samples are produced per GPU; users ask per job and per team. You choose, and must explain, where each key is used.

clarifications.q: What should a per-minute rollup hold?
clarifications.a: You decide. Averages alone are not enough for some questions, such as "was the GPU ever pegged at 100%?" or "did the error counter increase?".

clarifications.q: Can one GPU be held by several jobs at once?
clarifications.a: Yes, when it is split into slices. Whole-GPU metrics then belong to several jobs.

clarifications.q: How late can a scheduler event be?
clarifications.a: Usually seconds; occasionally several minutes, after a scheduler restart.

clarifications.q: Which clock is right?
clarifications.a: Neither perfectly. Scheduler timestamps come from one service; sample timestamps come from each node.

hints: Turn scheduler events into a table of holding intervals per GPU (gpu, slice, job, from, to). The join is then "which interval contains this second", which a sorted structure per GPU answers quickly.
Pick rollup aggregates that can be merged: sum and count, min and max, a histogram or sketch for percentiles, and first and last values for counters.
Treat an interval whose release has not arrived yet as open, and decide what the dashboard shows meanwhile and what the rollup does later.
followups: A release event arrives five minutes late. Which samples were joined to the wrong state, and how do you correct the dashboard and the rollups?
One node's clock is 4 minutes ahead. How would you detect it from the data, and what do you do with its samples?
Capacity planning asks for p95 utilisation per team per month. Which rollups give that exactly, which give it approximately, and which cannot?
The raw tier costs too much at {{gpus}} GPUs. What would you keep at full resolution, for whom, and for how long?
A job's slice layout changes mid-run. How does your interval table represent it, and what does the job's dashboard show?

rules.ask: The release event for a job arrives after its minute window closed. What does your window emit, and how is it corrected?
Your hourly rollup stores the average. How do you compute the daily p95 from it, and how would you know a GPU hit 100% for ten seconds?
How did you choose the lateness bound, given clock drift of {{clock_skew}}, and what happens to a sample beyond it?
The scheduler and the node never record the same second. What kind of join do you need, and how do you make it cheap?
An investigation needs the raw seconds from 40 days ago. What do you say, and what would you have kept to answer it?

incidents: After a scheduler restart, release events for 2% of jobs arrive eight minutes late; for those minutes, dashboards show the old jobs still running on GPUs that new jobs now hold.
A node's clock drifts by {{clock_skew}}, and its samples are joined to the job that held the GPU before the current one.
A rollup job is rerun after a bug fix, and its hourly utilisation for one week no longer matches what was already shown to teams.

templates.title: Training run lineage: restarts, resumed checkpoints and forks
templates.subtopic: lineage graphs, checkpoints, metric series across restarts and forks

sections.scenario: A team running training jobs on GPUs launches about {{runs_per_week}} runs a week. Long runs reach {{steps}} steps and save a checkpoint every {{checkpoint_every}}. Runs crash and are restarted from the last checkpoint, so some steps are trained twice. Researchers fork a run: they take a checkpoint, change a hyperparameter such as the learning rate, and continue as a new run. Each run logs {{metrics_per_step}} metrics per step. Researchers want one loss curve for "the run I care about", across every restart and back through the forks it came from, without the steps that were thrown away.
sections.problem: Design the data model and the pipeline for training-run lineage. Cover the entities (run, attempt, checkpoint, fork, configuration), how a restart and a fork are recorded, which step of which attempt is the "effective" one when steps were trained twice, how a metric series is assembled for a run across its whole lineage, how configurations and their differences are stored, ingestion of {{metrics_per_step}} metrics per step, and the queries researchers run most often.
sections.constraints: Metrics arrive from running jobs and can be duplicated when a logger retries. A crashed attempt's metrics after its last checkpoint must stay visible for debugging, but must not appear in the effective curve. A fork can start from any checkpoint, including one from a run that was later deleted from the dashboard. Comparing two forks from the same parent must be quick.
sections.assumptions: All volumes and intervals are hypothetical. Each job reports a run id, an attempt number, the checkpoint it resumed from (if any), its configuration and its metrics with step numbers. Checkpoint files live in object storage; this design stores their metadata, not the files.
sections.criteria: Clear entities for run, attempt, checkpoint, fork and configuration; metrics kept per attempt and the effective view computed from attempt ranges and fork edges; superseded steps kept and labelled; idempotent ingestion on (run, attempt, step, metric); configuration differences queryable; lineage queries that stay fast (precomputed effective segments, downsampled curves that keep extremes); deletion as a soft state that preserves lineage; access rules across teams; a plan for each incident.

clarifications.q: What is an attempt?
clarifications.a: One execution of a run, from start or resume until it ends or crashes. A run has one or more attempts.

clarifications.q: Steps 4 001 to 4 350 were trained by attempt 1, which crashed, and again by attempt 2, which resumed from the checkpoint at step 4 000. Which count?
clarifications.a: Attempt 2's. Attempt 1's are kept for debugging but are not effective.

clarifications.q: Does a fork share history with its parent?
clarifications.a: Yes, up to the checkpoint it started from. After that it is its own run.

clarifications.q: Can a run resume from a checkpoint that is not the latest?
clarifications.a: Yes, for example when the latest is corrupt. Everything after the checkpoint used is superseded.

clarifications.q: How are configurations compared?
clarifications.a: Researchers want to see exactly which values differ between two runs, including nested ones.

hints: Model lineage as a graph of segments: each attempt covers a range of steps starting from a checkpoint, and a fork is an edge from a checkpoint of one run to the start of another.
The effective step s of a run is from the latest attempt whose range covers s, walking back through the fork edges for steps before the fork point.
Store metrics by (run, attempt, step) once and compute the effective view on top, rather than rewriting metrics when an attempt crashes.
followups: A researcher deletes a parent run from the dashboard. What happens to its forks' curves, and what do you keep?
A checkpoint turns out to be corrupt, and three runs were forked from it. How do you find them, and what do you tell their owners?
Comparing two forks at {{steps}} steps with {{metrics_per_step}} metrics each is slow. What do you precompute or downsample, and how do you keep the shape of a loss spike?
Two attempts of the same run used different library versions. Where does that show up, and how would a researcher see that the curve changed character at the restart?
Lineage spans many teams' runs. Who may see a fork of their run made by another team, and how is that enforced?

rules.ask: Attempt 1 crashed at step 4 350 and attempt 2 overwrote steps 4 001 to 4 350. How does an engineer now debug why attempt 1 crashed?
A fork starts from step 30 000 of a parent that itself was resumed twice. Walk me through the query that builds the fork's curve from step 0.
How do you show the exact differences between the configurations of two forks, including nested values, and how do you search for every run with a given learning rate?
A logger retries a batch of metrics for steps 9 000 to 9 100. What key makes the retry harmless, and does it differ from the key that picks the effective step?
A new metric appears in half the runs. What does your table do, and how do you query a metric that most runs lack?

incidents: A job is restarted from a checkpoint {{checkpoint_every}} older than the latest because the latest is corrupt, and the effective curve briefly shows both attempts' values for the same steps.
A logger retries after a network timeout and sends {{metrics_per_step}} metrics for 500 steps twice; one researcher's loss curve shows a sawtooth.
A popular parent run is deleted from the dashboard, and the curves of its forks lose their first 30 000 steps.

templates.title: GPU partition layouts over time — slices, the jobs they ran and utilisation per physical GPU
templates.subtopic: partitioned GPUs, layout history, slice identity, weighted utilisation

sections.scenario: A GPU cluster operator rents out {{gpus}} data-centre GPUs, either whole or partitioned into isolated slices. In this exercise a GPU can be split into at most {{slices_per_gpu}} fixed-size slices, each a multiple of 1/{{slices_per_gpu}} of the GPU, using one of a small catalogue of layouts the operator defines (for example one whole GPU, or a half plus two quarters). A layout can be changed only while the GPU is empty, and the scheduler changes layouts about {{reconfigs_per_day}} times a day to fit the queue. Each slice runs at most one job at a time. A telemetry exporter emits a utilisation sample every {{sample_seconds}} seconds per slice, labelled with the GPU serial number and the slice's position index on that GPU; after a reconfiguration the positions start again from 0. Teams are charged by slice-hours, and capacity planning wants to know how busy each physical GPU really was and how much capacity sat stranded in slices too small for the jobs waiting.
sections.problem: Design the data model. Cover: physical GPUs; the layout catalogue (slice sizes and positions); the history of which layout each GPU had and when; slice instances with an identity that survives reconfiguration; job allocations to slices; and utilisation samples joined to the slice instance and job that produced them. Show how the model answers: "which job ran on GPU G, position P at time T", "utilisation per physical GPU per hour, weighted by slice size, counting idle slices and unpartitioned time", "slice-hours per team per month", and "hours each GPU spent in each layout, and stranded slice capacity per hour".
sections.constraints: A slice instance id is never reused, even when a new layout puts a slice at the same position. Utilisation per physical GPU must account for every slice and for time with no job. Samples can arrive up to 15 minutes late and out of order. Chargeback for a closed month changes only through a documented adjustment. History is kept for 13 months.
sections.assumptions: GPU counts, slice counts, layouts, sample intervals and reconfiguration rates are hypothetical and this exercise's own, not a description of any product's partitioning rules. A slice's utilisation sample is a percentage of that slice's own capacity. Clocks on the nodes are synchronised to within a second.
sections.criteria: GPU, layout catalogue, layout history and slice instances separated, with slice ids never reused; samples resolved from (serial, position, time) to a slice instance through the layout interval; allocations as intervals on slice instances; size-weighted utilisation with idle slices and gaps as zero; half-open intervals and a stated rule for late samples; chargeback from allocations, not samples, with month-close adjustments; a precise stranded-capacity definition; each incident contained, corrected and guarded.

clarifications.q: Can a job span several slices?
clarifications.a: No. A job asks for one slice of a given size; multi-GPU jobs use whole GPUs, which are a one-slice layout.

clarifications.q: What does the exporter send during a reconfiguration?
clarifications.a: Nothing for that GPU until the new layout is up; the gap lasts seconds to minutes.

clarifications.q: How is a whole GPU represented?
clarifications.a: Your choice, but the same queries must work for whole and partitioned GPUs. A one-slice layout is a common answer.

clarifications.q: Is a slice with no job billed?
clarifications.a: No. Teams pay for allocated slice-hours only; idle slices are the operator's cost and belong in the utilisation and stranded-capacity numbers.

clarifications.q: What does stranded mean here?
clarifications.a: Free slice capacity on a GPU at a time when every waiting job asked for a larger slice than any free slice on that GPU. Define it precisely in your answer.

hints: Separate three things that change at different rates: the layout catalogue (rarely), a GPU's layout history (minutes to hours), and allocations of jobs to slices (minutes).
The exporter's (serial, position) is a label, not an identity. Resolve it to a slice instance through the layout interval that contains the sample's time.
Weight each slice's utilisation by its size and give idle slices and gaps a utilisation of 0, or the per-GPU number describes only the busy part.
followups: Write the query, against your model, for "which job ran on GPU G, position 1 at 14:05". What makes it correct across a reconfiguration at 14:00?

A GPU had a half plus two quarters from 10:00 to 10:40, with only the half busy at 100%, then one whole slice idle until 11:00. What is its utilisation for 10:00–11:00, and how does your model get it?
Samples arrive up to 15 minutes late, and some arrive after a reconfiguration. How do you attribute a late sample, and when is an hour's number final?
At {{gpus}} GPUs with samples every {{sample_seconds}} seconds per slice, what do you keep raw, for how long, and what rollups serve the dashboards and chargeback?
Define stranded capacity as a query. Which inputs does it need from the queue, and how would the scheduler team use it to choose layouts?

rules.ask: The layout changed at 14:00 and position 0 now belongs to a different slice and job. Which key does a 14:01 sample carry, and how does your model attribute it?
One quarter-slice is at 100% and three quarters are idle. What does your average say about the GPU, and how do you weight it?
Your layout history is effective-dated. Is the end of one interval the same instant as the start of the next, and which interval owns a sample at exactly that instant?
If the GPU row holds only the current layout, how do you answer which job ran on position 1 last Tuesday?
A job ran from 23:50 to 00:20 across a month end that was then closed. How are its slice-hours split, and what happens if a late sample changes them?

incidents: After a reconfiguration the exporter reported the new layout's first slice at position 0, the same label as the previous layout's half slice. A model joined on (serial, position) billed an hour of a new team's job to the team whose job ended just before the change.

The fleet dashboard showed one pool at 90% utilisation while most of its GPUs had one busy small slice and the others idle: it averaged only the slices that sent samples and gave each the same weight.

With about {{reconfigs_per_day}} layout changes a day, a scheduler release changed layouts on busy GPUs by mistake. Jobs were killed, and the layout history shows a layout change inside a running allocation.

templates.title: Node and GPU inventory — serials in slots, firmware, burn-in and service state as of a date
templates.subtopic: asset identity versus position, effective-dated components, observed versus planned state

sections.scenario: A GPU cluster operator runs {{nodes}} GPU servers, each with {{gpus_per_node}} GPU slots, network adapters, a baseboard and power supplies. Components move: a GPU that fails is pulled for repair (about {{rma_per_week}} returns a week), a repaired or new GPU goes into whichever slot needs it, and whole nodes move between racks. Each node carries {{firmware_components}} firmware components (for example GPU, baseboard and network adapter firmware) that are updated in rolling waves. A new or repaired node runs a burn-in suite of stress tests before it enters service, and a node in service can be drained for repair or maintenance and later returned. Reliability engineers ask questions such as "which GPU serials were in node N on 3 March", "failure rate by firmware version", "how many nodes passed burn-in on the first attempt" and "how long do drained nodes take to return".
sections.problem: Design the inventory model. Cover: assets with their own identity (GPU, node, adapter, baseboard) and where each was installed over time; firmware versions per component over time, distinguishing what a rollout intended from what the device reported; burn-in runs and their test results, including retests; and the node service lifecycle (received, burn-in, in service, drained, under repair, retired) with reasons. Show the queries for: the components and firmware of a node as of any date; the failure rate per firmware version with a correct denominator; first-attempt burn-in pass rate per month; and drain-to-return time per reason.
sections.constraints: History is never overwritten: any past state must be answerable. An asset's history follows the asset, not the slot it is in. Firmware state for analysis must be what the device reported, not what was planned. Corrections to recorded history (a wrong serial typed during a swap) must be possible without losing what was believed at the time.
sections.assumptions: Node counts, slot counts, component lists and return rates are hypothetical. Every component has a readable serial number. Devices report their firmware versions to an agent on the node every few minutes while the node is up.
sections.criteria: Assets separate from positions, installations as intervals; firmware as reported observations compressed into intervals, kept apart from rollout intent; burn-in runs and test results as append-only rows with attempt numbers; lifecycle state as intervals with reasons; valid time and recorded time (or an equivalent correction log); correct denominators (component-days exposed per firmware version); as-of queries with half-open intervals; each incident contained, corrected and guarded.

clarifications.q: Do GPUs ever move between nodes without going through repair?
clarifications.a: Yes. Technicians sometimes swap GPUs between nodes to isolate a fault.

clarifications.q: Who records a swap?
clarifications.a: A technician's work order says which serial was removed and which was installed; the node agent later reports the serials it actually sees. They can disagree.

clarifications.q: What is a retest?
clarifications.a: A burn-in suite run again on the same node after a fix. Keep every run; the question asks about the first attempt.

clarifications.q: Is "as of" the date the change happened or the date we learned about it?
clarifications.a: Both matter. Say which question each answers and whether your model can give both.

clarifications.q: Is a firmware rollout instantaneous per node?
clarifications.a: No. An update can fail and leave the old version, or need a reboot before the new version is active.

hints: Separate the asset (serial) from its position (node and slot), and record installations as intervals that link the two.
Keep the reported firmware versions as observations with times, and the rollout's intention as a separate record; derive "running version" intervals from observations.
Valid time (when it was true) and recorded time (when the inventory learned it) answer different questions; a correction is a new record, not an edit.
followups: Write the as-of query for "GPU serials and firmware versions in node N on date D". Which intervals are half-open?
A work order says GPU A replaced GPU B in slot 3, but the node agent reports serial C. How do you store both, and which does the as-of query return?
Define failure rate per GPU firmware version so that a version deployed for two days is not compared unfairly with one deployed for two months.
A node failed burn-in twice and passed on the third run after a GPU swap. What are its first-attempt result, its burn-in time, and which GPU does the failure history attach to?
At {{nodes}} nodes with firmware observations every few minutes, how do you store reported versions without keeping billions of identical rows?

rules.ask: A GPU was moved from node 7 slot 2 into node 9 slot 5 after repair. Where does its error history live in your model, and does the new GPU in node 7 slot 2 inherit anything?
The rollout updated the plan, but 3% of devices failed the update silently. What does your column say about them, and how would you know?
A technician corrects a serial typed wrongly last week. Do you change the old interval or add a record, and can you still say what the inventory believed last week?
Is the denominator nodes or burn-in runs? How do retests and nodes still in burn-in at month end affect it?

incidents: A repaired GPU went into a different node. The inventory kept failure history by (node, slot), so the new GPU in the old slot inherited the old one's error history and was drained, while the repaired GPU appeared to have a clean record.

A firmware rollout to {{nodes}} nodes was recorded from the rollout plan. Some nodes failed the update and kept the old version; a failure analysis by firmware version blamed the new version for failures on nodes that never ran it.
Burn-in retests overwrote the first result, so the first-attempt pass rate rose from 82% to 97% in one month without any change on the floor.

templates.title: Software stack provenance per job — reproducing a training performance regression
templates.subtopic: immutable image digests, host versus container components, run-time observation, stack diffs

sections.scenario: A team runs about {{jobs_per_day}} training and evaluation jobs a day on a GPU cluster with {{node_pools}} node pools. A job's performance depends on a stack of software: the GPU driver and firmware on the host; the container image (about {{images}} distinct images are in use), which carries a GPU programming toolkit such as CUDA, math and collective-communication libraries and a training framework; host libraries mounted into the container; environment variables and launch flags; and the job's own code and configuration. Job specifications reference images by tag, and tags move. Drivers are upgraded pool by pool. Last week a model's step time became {{regression}} slower than the week before, and nobody can say what changed between the two runs.
sections.problem: Design the provenance model that lets anyone reproduce and explain a run. Cover: images identified immutably, with their component inventory (packages and versions); the host stack per node over time (driver, firmware, mounted libraries); the resolved stack per job run and per node it ran on, as observed at run time; the job's code version, configuration and launch flags; and performance results per run. Show how the model answers: "what exactly ran in job J", "which components differ between run A and run B", "which runs used library version V", and "did the step-time change follow a stack change or something else".
sections.constraints: A run's provenance is recorded once and never changes. Tags are not identities. A multi-node job may run on nodes with different host stacks, and that must be visible. Recording provenance must not add more than a few seconds to job start. Configuration values that are secrets are never stored.
sections.assumptions: Job, image and pool counts and the regression size are hypothetical. Images are built by a pipeline that can emit a component list. A small agent in each job can report loaded library versions and host details at start-up.
sections.criteria: Images by digest with a component inventory stored once; host stack as effective-dated per node; observed per-node provenance at run time kept apart from declared; normalised (component, version) rows that make diffs and "which runs used V" queries; code commit, configuration and flags captured with secrets excluded; hardware in the diff; performance linked to runs; mixed-stack jobs visible; each incident contained, corrected and guarded.

clarifications.q: Is the image component list enough?
clarifications.a: No. A host-mounted library or an environment variable can change what is actually loaded. Say how you capture what ran, not only what was shipped.

clarifications.q: Do we need every package in the image?
clarifications.a: Store them all once per image digest; jobs reference the digest.

clarifications.q: Are the two runs the same code?
clarifications.a: The same repository, but possibly different commits and configuration. Your diff should show that too.

clarifications.q: Do runs on different hardware count?
clarifications.a: Yes. Two pools can have different GPU generations or interconnects; the diff must include hardware.

clarifications.q: What performance data exists?
clarifications.a: Per-step times and throughput reported by the training loop, plus job start and end.

hints: Identify images by content digest and store the tag only as an observation of what the tag pointed to when the job resolved it.
Separate declared provenance (spec, image manifest) from observed provenance (what the agent saw on each node at start-up), and keep both.
A diff between two runs is a comparison of two sets of (component, version) pairs; normalise the stack into rows so diffs are queries.
followups: Write the query that lists components whose version differs between run A and run B, including components present in only one.
One 64-node job ran on two driver versions because a pool was mid-upgrade. How does your model show it, and how should step-time comparisons treat it?
The image tag was moved to a new build between the two runs. What did each run record, and how do you prove which image ran?
How would you find every run in the last month that loaded collective-communication library version V, at {{jobs_per_day}} jobs a day?
The step-time change did not coincide with any stack change. What else in your model would you check, and what is missing from it?

rules.ask: The tag your job spec names was rebuilt between run A and run B. What does your model record for each run, and can you tell the two images apart?
A library mounted from the host overrides the one in the image. Where does your model see that?
You store the stack as one document per run. How do you answer "which runs used library version V" across a month without scanning every document?
A multi-node job ran on nodes with two different driver versions. Does your job-level record show that, or only one of them?

incidents: A model's step time became {{regression}} slower. The job spec named the same image tag both weeks, but the tag had been rebuilt with a newer communication library; the run records had only the tag.

A rolling driver upgrade across {{node_pools}} pools left one large job running on two driver versions; the provenance record took the first node's versions and the regression analysis compared it as if it were uniform.
A host-mounted library was upgraded on one pool. Images were unchanged, so a provenance model built from image manifests showed identical stacks for a fast run and a slow one.

templates.title: Interconnect fabric topology over time — switches, ports, cables and link flaps
templates.subtopic: physical topology as a versioned graph, link state history, placement and fault queries

sections.scenario: A GPU cluster operator connects {{nodes}} GPU nodes with a {{tiers}}-tier switched fabric. Each node has {{nics_per_node}} network adapters, each cabled to a leaf switch port; leaves connect up to the next tier. Physical changes are routine: cables are replaced, ports are re-cabled, a failed switch is replaced by a new one in the same position, and nodes move. Links also flap (go down and come back) and accumulate error counters; on a bad day the fabric reports about {{flap_events_per_day}} link state events. Two groups use the topology: the scheduler wants to place a job's nodes as close together as possible ("under the same leaf" or "within one hop of the same spine"), and the reliability team asks which jobs had nodes behind a link that flapped or a switch that was replaced, at the time it happened.
sections.problem: Design the data model for the fabric as it changes. Cover: devices (nodes, adapters, switches) with physical identity separate from logical position; ports; cables; links as connections between two ports over a time interval; link state changes and error counters; and how the model serves both a current topology snapshot for placement and historical questions. Show how it answers: "which leaf and spine served node N's adapter k on date D", "the nodes under each leaf right now", "jobs with a node behind link L while it flapped", and "links that flapped more than K times in a day, with the cable and switch involved".
sections.constraints: Topology history is never overwritten. A replaced switch keeps its position and name but is a different device. The current snapshot must be readable by the scheduler in milliseconds. Link state events arrive at least once and can be out of order by up to a minute. The model must detect impossible states (one port connected to two cables at once).
sections.assumptions: Node, tier, adapter and event counts are hypothetical, and the topology is this exercise's own, not a description of any product's reference architecture. Switches report link state changes and per-port counters; cabling changes are recorded by technicians and, separately, discovered by a neighbour-discovery protocol that reports which port sees which peer.
sections.criteria: Devices, ports, cables and links as separate entities; physical identity apart from position and names; links as effective-dated port pairs carried by cables; reconciliation of technician records with discovered neighbours and a check for impossible states; link state as deduplicated events with derived intervals and a flap definition; a materialised current snapshot for placement; counter resets handled per device; historical job-to-link questions answered with as-of joins; each incident contained, corrected and guarded.

clarifications.q: Is a link the same as a cable?
clarifications.a: No. A cable can be moved to other ports; a link is "this port connected to that port" for an interval, and it is carried by a cable.

clarifications.q: Which is the source of truth for cabling, technicians or discovery?
clarifications.a: Neither alone. Discovery reports what is physically connected when the link is up; technicians record intent. Say how you reconcile them.

clarifications.q: What is a flap?
clarifications.a: A down followed by an up on the same link within this exercise's 60 seconds. Longer outages are outages.

clarifications.q: How does the scheduler use the topology?
clarifications.a: It needs, per node, the leaf of each adapter and the next tier above, refreshed within a minute of a change.

clarifications.q: Do we model the switch's internals?
clarifications.a: No. Ports and the links between them are enough.

hints: Separate physical identity (switch serial, cable id) from logical position (rack, slot, switch name) and link the two with effective-dated rows.
Keep link state as an append-only event table deduplicated by (link, timestamp, state), and derive intervals of up and down from it.
Serve the scheduler from a materialised current snapshot derived from the history, not from the history tables directly.
followups: Write the query for "jobs with a node behind link L between its first and last flap on date D", against your model and a job allocation table.
A technician swapped two cables and recorded the swap on the wrong ports. Discovery reports something else. What does your model show, and which record wins?
A failed spine switch was replaced at 03:00 by a new device with the same name. How do "error counters for spine S this month" and "flaps per device" differ in your model?
At {{flap_events_per_day}} link events a day, how do you store raw events, derived intervals and daily summaries, and for how long?
How would you compute, for every pair of nodes, whether they share a leaf on any adapter, without materialising all pairs at {{nodes}} nodes?

rules.ask: The scheduler needs a snapshot in milliseconds and reliability needs history for months. Does one graph store serve both, and how do you version edges over time?
An edge changes when a cable moves. Is your edge row updated or closed and replaced, and how do you answer which leaf served a node last month?
The replaced spine kept its name. If your keys are names, how do you keep the old device's error history apart from the new one's?
Your flap count comes from raw events. What happens to it when the feed redelivers a minute of events, or delivers a down after its up?

incidents: A technician recorded a cable swap on the wrong ports. For two days the model showed one adapter connected to two leaves, and the scheduler placed jobs it believed were under one leaf across two.

One flapping port produced about a third of the day's {{flap_events_per_day}} link events. The nightly job that rebuilt the topology snapshot from raw events ran past its window, and the scheduler used a day-old snapshot.

A spine switch was replaced in place and kept its name. Its error counters restarted from 0, and a dashboard that computed per-switch error deltas by name showed a large negative rate and hid the new switch's errors.

templates.title: Jobs placed on a failing node — between the first fatal error and the drain
templates.subtopic: event state machines, exposure windows, interval joins, distinct counting, effective-dated membership

sections.scenario: A GPU cluster operator runs training jobs on clusters {{cluster_list}}. The GPU driver on each node reports Xid-style error events, each with a numeric xid_code; this exercise's lookup xid_codes says whether a code is fatal or a warning (the codes and their severities are hypothetical).
