Health checks are not instant: after a fatal error, a node keeps accepting new jobs until an operator or an automated check drains it. {{lifecycle_rule}} The reliability team wants to know, per cluster, how many jobs the scheduler placed on nodes in that gap, because those jobs started on a GPU that had already failed.
sections.problem: Write one PostgreSQL query that returns cluster, nodes_affected, jobs_placed, jobs_failed: one row per cluster with at least one job placed in an exposure window, ordered by cluster. An exposure window on a node opens at a fatal error event (an xid event whose code has severity fatal) that occurs while the node is in service and no window is open, and closes at the node's next drain event; if there is no later drain, it is still open. Further fatal errors inside an open window change nothing. {{episode_rule}} A job was placed in a window if one of its allocations on that node has started_at at or after the window opens and strictly before it closes. jobs_placed counts distinct jobs, nodes_affected counts distinct nodes with such a placement, and jobs_failed counts distinct placed jobs whose final_state is failed. Count each placement in the cluster the node was assigned to when the allocation started (node_assignments, half-open [assigned_from, assigned_until), NULL meaning still assigned). {{cluster_rule}}
sections.constraints: One SQL statement (CTEs and window functions allowed). The window includes its opening instant and excludes its closing instant. A job already running when the fatal error arrived was not placed in the window. The sample has {{events}} node events and {{allocations}} job allocations; production has billions of error events and millions of jobs a month.
sections.assumptions: Hypothetical schema, clusters, node ids, codes and times. No two events on the same node share a timestamp. A drain with no fatal error before it is a maintenance drain and opens nothing. Warning-severity events never open a window.
sections.criteria: Only fatal-severity events open windows (via the lookup); windows opened only from in service and closed by the next drain; at Hard and above, several windows per node with resumes, a fatal error while drained ignored, and open windows kept; half-open placement on started_at; distinct jobs and nodes; the cluster as assigned at the allocation's start; deterministic ordering; can discuss confirmation lag, incremental windows and alerting without paging on maintenance.

clarifications.q: Does a job that started exactly at the fatal error count?
clarifications.a: Yes. The window opens at that instant.

clarifications.q: And one that started exactly at the drain?
clarifications.a: No. The drain closes the window at that instant.

clarifications.q: A two-node job had both of its nodes in exposure windows. How many jobs is that?
clarifications.a: One job. Both nodes count in nodes_affected.

clarifications.q: Is a job that was already running at the fatal error placed in the window?
clarifications.a: No. It was hit by the failure, which is a different question; this one asks what the scheduler placed after the failure.

clarifications.q: Should I use nodes.cluster?
clarifications.a: It is the node's current cluster. The rule is the assignment at the allocation's start time.

hints: Reduce the events to the ones that matter (fatal errors, drains and, where present, resumes) and walk them per node in time order: a window is the first fatal error after the node last came into service, up to the next drain.

A running count of drain and resume events per node splits the timeline into segments; in a segment that began in service, the first fatal error opens the window and the start of the next segment closes it.
Join allocations to windows on node and a half-open time range, then attach the cluster with a second half-open range join, and count DISTINCT ids.
followups: Add the median minutes from the first fatal error to the drain per cluster. Which windows are excluded, and why?
The scheduler team says a drain takes effect only when the node agent confirms it, up to 2 minutes later. How would you change the window's end, and what data would you need?
At billions of error events, how would you keep exposure windows up to date incrementally instead of re-walking every node's history?
Turn this into an alert: what would page, on which threshold, and how do you avoid paging on maintenance drains?

rules.ask: A node failed, was drained, returned to service and failed again. What does the minimum fatal time per node give you for the second failure?
A two-node job had both nodes in exposure windows, and a requeued job has two attempts. What does your count say for each?
A node was moved to another cluster during its repair. Which cluster does a job placed on it last week belong to in your query?
A node failed and has not been drained yet. Does your join keep its window, and is it the one reliability most needs to see?
Why does a job that started before the fatal error and ended after it not count here? Which question would it answer?

incidents: The automated drain ran only on an hourly health sweep, so nodes stayed in service for up to an hour after a fatal error. This report showed dozens of jobs a day placed on failing nodes, most of which failed within minutes and were requeued, sometimes onto the same node.

A driver update reclassified one code from warning to fatal in the lookup. The next run of this report rewrote last month's numbers; the team had to decide whether to version the lookup by effective date.

During a repair wave, several nodes were moved to another cluster while drained. The weekly report attributed their earlier failures to the cluster they had just joined, until it switched to node_assignments.

templates.title: Failing-GPU detection with drain decisions you can audit
templates.subtopic: signal fusion, automated remediation, audit, measured false positives

sections.scenario: A GPU cluster operator runs {{gpus}} GPUs in nodes of {{gpus_per_node}}, shared by many teams' training and inference jobs. A GPU that is going bad rarely announces it cleanly. Its correctable memory-error counter climbs; it may log driver error events with numeric codes ("Xid-style" events in this exercise), some of which point at the hardware and some at the application; its interconnect links may count errors; and jobs that use it fail, often as timeouts on every rank of a large job rather than as an error on the GPU itself. Per-GPU counters are sampled every {{sample_interval}}. When a node is suspected, it can be drained: no new jobs are placed on it, running jobs are checkpointed or killed, and an active diagnostic suite runs before the node returns to service or goes to repair.
sections.problem: Design the failing-GPU detection and drain system. Cover the signals and how they are collected and normalised; how a job failure is attributed to a node (or not); the detection rules and how they are versioned and rolled out; the drain decision, automatic or by a person, and the limits on it; the audit trail that lets anyone see, months later, why a node was drained; return to service; and how you measure false positives (healthy nodes drained) and false negatives (bad nodes left in service).
sections.constraints: No more than {{drain_budget}} of nodes may be drained automatically at any time; beyond that a person must approve. A fatal hardware event should lead to a drain decision within five minutes. Draining a node interrupts the jobs on it, and a large job may span hundreds of nodes. Counters are cumulative and reset when the driver reloads. Every drain must record which signals, which rule and which rule version caused it.
sections.assumptions: All counts, thresholds and timings are hypothetical, as is this exercise's mapping of event codes to hardware or application causes. The scheduler publishes job events (start, end, exit reason, the nodes and GPUs used). The diagnostic suite takes about an hour and is good but not perfect: it can miss intermittent faults.
sections.criteria: Normalised signals with counter-reset-safe deltas and event-code mapping that is versioned; job-failure attribution that looks for the first or the hardware-implicated rank and does not blame every node in a failed job; rules versioned, shadow-tested and compared on labelled outcomes; drain actions behind budgets, rate limits and correlated-cause grouping, with human approval beyond the budget; checkpoint-aware drains for large jobs; a complete audit record per decision; return to service with probation; false-positive and false-negative rates defined against a stated ground truth and tracked over time; adapts to each incident with diagnosis, recovery and prevention.

clarifications.q: Is there a ground truth for "this GPU was bad"?
clarifications.a: Partly: a failed diagnostic, a repair ticket that replaced a part, or a recurrence after return to service. Decide how you combine them.

clarifications.q: Can a user's code cause the same symptoms as bad hardware?
clarifications.a: Yes. Out-of-memory errors, illegal memory accesses and deadlocks in user code all produce job failures, and some produce driver events.

clarifications.q: Do failures cluster?
clarifications.a: Sometimes: a switch, a power distribution unit, a cooling fault or a bad driver rollout can affect many nodes at once.

clarifications.q: Who owns the drain decision today?
clarifications.a: An on-call engineer, by hand, from dashboards. You are designing what replaces or assists them.

clarifications.q: Can we drain a single GPU rather than a node?
clarifications.a: In this exercise, scheduling is per node for large jobs and per GPU for small ones; you decide whether a single-GPU drain is worth supporting.

hints: Separate three things: collecting and normalising signals, deciding (rules with versions), and acting (drains with budgets and approvals). Each needs its own audit.
A collective-communication timeout is seen on every rank of the job. Look for the rank or node that stopped first, or that logged a hardware event, before blaming any of them.
Many nodes failing at once is usually one shared cause, not many bad GPUs. Group by what they share before you drain.
followups: Walk through one fatal event on one GPU: what is recorded, which rule fires, what the scheduler does to the running job, and what the audit record contains.
A large job fails with a timeout on all of its ranks. How does your system decide which node, if any, is to blame?
How do you roll out a new detection rule without risking a mass drain, and how do you know it is better than the old one?
How do you measure the false-positive and false-negative rates when the diagnostic suite itself misses some faults?
Fifty nodes in one rack row report errors within ten minutes. Walk through what the system does, automatically and with people.

rules.ask: How do you get labels for training it, and how does the on-call engineer find out why the model drained a particular node?
The counter resets when the driver reloads. How does your threshold see a GPU that gains a thousand errors between every reload?
Draining that node kills a job running on 300 nodes that has not checkpointed for two hours. Who decides, and on what information?
What stops your automation from draining a quarter of the cluster when a driver update makes a harmless event appear everywhere?
Six months later a team says a drain cost them a deadline. What exactly can you show them about why it happened?

incidents: A driver update reaches a fifth of the nodes and makes a harmless event code appear at every job start. Within an hour the detector proposes draining far more than {{drain_budget}} of the nodes.

A large training job fails four times in a day with collective-communication timeouts. Each time the detector drains a different node; diagnostics on all four pass. The real cause is one flapping link on a switch port.

A GPU's correctable memory-error count rises by several hundred between every driver reload, which happens nightly, so its cumulative counter never crosses the threshold. It is found only after it corrupts a checkpoint.
Diagnostics pass on 40% of the nodes the system drained last month. One team says the rules are too eager; another says the diagnostics miss intermittent faults. Both could be right.

templates.title: Straggler-aware observability for training jobs across thousands of ranks
templates.subtopic: per-rank telemetry, stragglers, collective waits

sections.scenario: Teams run large synchronous training jobs on a GPU cluster; the largest uses {{ranks}} ranks (one process per GPU) and takes about {{step_time}} per step, and about {{jobs}} large jobs run at once. Jobs combine data, tensor and pipeline parallelism, so ranks have different roles: a pipeline's first and last stages do different work from its middle stages. Every step, ranks compute, then wait for each other in collective operations such as all-reduce. One slow rank (a throttled GPU, a bad link, a noisy neighbour on the host, a slow data loader) makes every other rank wait, and the whole job slows. Engineers want to see per-step timings, find stragglers quickly, and compare a job with its own history.
sections.problem: Design the observability system: what each rank measures and emits per step; how it is aggregated and stored without shipping every number from every rank at full fidelity forever; how stragglers are detected and attributed to a rank, a node, a switch or a data source; the dashboards and alerts; and how a job is compared with its own earlier runs. Say what the telemetry costs the training job.
sections.constraints: Telemetry may slow training by no more than {{overhead}}. A persistent straggler must be identified within 100 steps. Node clocks differ by up to several milliseconds, and a node in trouble may stop reporting. Each rank knows its role (data-parallel index, tensor-parallel index, pipeline stage) and its node; the cluster's topology (node to switch) is available from inventory.
sections.assumptions: All sizes, rates and budgets are hypothetical. Ranks can time their own phases with local clocks: compute, waiting in each collective, waiting for input data, optimiser step and checkpoint writes.
sections.criteria: Per-rank phase durations measured on local clocks, with collective wait separated from compute and data wait; straggler detection by least wait or most compute within ranks of the same role; topology-aware attribution (GPU, node, switch, storage) by grouping slow ranks by shared component; volume estimate with node or job-level aggregation and full fidelity only for samples and anomaly windows; the cost of telemetry itself measured against the budget; baselines per job and comparison with its own history; careful use of clocks for timelines; alerts with owners and actions; adapts to each incident with diagnosis, recovery and prevention.

clarifications.q: Do we need every rank's timings for every step?
clarifications.a: You decide; say what you keep at full fidelity, for how long, and what you summarise.

clarifications.q: Are all ranks expected to take the same time?
clarifications.a: Only ranks with the same role. Pipeline stages and tensor shards can legitimately differ.

clarifications.q: Can the system act on a straggler, or only report it?
clarifications.a: Reporting is required; proposing a node replacement to the job owner is welcome; you decide about anything automatic.

clarifications.q: Is the profiler available?
clarifications.a: Yes, but it is heavy; it can be switched on for a few steps on chosen ranks.

hints: In a synchronous step, the straggler is the rank that waits least in the collective; everyone else's wait is inflated by it. High wait everywhere is a symptom, not the cause.
Durations measured on one rank's own clock are safe to compare across ranks; absolute timestamps from different nodes are not.
Aggregate on the node or in the job (per-step min, median, max and the rank holding each), and keep full detail only for sampled steps and around anomalies.
followups: Estimate the telemetry volume for the largest job and for the whole cluster, and show where you cut it down.
Walk through how your system names the straggler in a {{ranks}}-rank job that slowed down by 30% an hour ago.
How do you distinguish one slow GPU from a slow switch that affects every node behind it, and from a slow shared file system feeding the data loaders?
How do you avoid flagging the first and last pipeline stages as stragglers on every step?
A job owner wants an automatic restart without the straggling node when one is found. What would have to be true before you allow it?

rules.ask: Node clocks differ by several milliseconds and a collective takes a few milliseconds. How does your timeline avoid showing a collective finishing before it started?
One rank in {{ranks}} is 40% slower. What does the average per-rank step time show, and what does the job actually experience?
How many distinct series does a per-rank, per-phase metric create across {{jobs}} jobs, and what does that do to your metrics store?
The straggler appears for two steps in every fifty. Does your sampling catch it, and how do you know?
Who is paged for a straggler in a team's job at 3 a.m., and what can they do about it?

incidents: Step time on a {{ranks}}-rank job rises 30%. The dashboard shows every rank spending most of each step waiting in collectives, and the on-call engineer spends two hours investigating the network before anyone checks which rank waits least.

An update to the telemetry agent makes each rank flush its metrics synchronously at the end of every step. Step time rises about 4% on every job, well above the {{overhead}} budget, and no alert fires because the agent's own cost is not measured.
The straggler alert fires on every step for the last pipeline stage of every job using pipeline parallelism, and teams start muting it.

A slow shared file system makes data-loader waits spike on a third of the ranks every few minutes. The straggler detector names a different node each time and the job owner drains three healthy nodes.

templates.title: Fair-share GPU accounting: promised, delivered, borrowed and preempted
templates.subtopic: quotas, decayed usage, preemption, reconciliation

sections.scenario: A GPU cluster of {{gpus}} GPUs is shared by {{teams}} teams. Each team is promised a guaranteed number of GPUs for the {{period}}. When a team does not use its guarantee, others may borrow the idle GPUs at lower priority; when the owner comes back, borrowed jobs are preempted after a short grace period in which they can checkpoint. Among queued jobs, the scheduler orders teams by fair-share priority, computed from each team's recent usage decayed with a half-life of {{half_life}}. Some jobs use whole GPUs and some use fixed-size slices of a partitioned GPU. Team leads and finance want to know, per team: what was promised, what was delivered, what was borrowed and lent, how much work was lost to preemption, and why a particular job waited.
sections.problem: Design the accounting system. Cover the event sources (scheduler job events, preemptions, quota grants and changes with effective dates, node availability); the usage ledger and its unit (GPU-seconds, with slices weighted); the definition of "delivered" against "promised"; the decayed-usage computation, reproducible for any past moment; the reports and chargeback; and the "why did my job wait?" explanation. Show how the numbers reconcile.
sections.constraints: Totals must reconcile every hour: GPU-seconds used by all teams, plus idle, plus unavailable (drained or in maintenance), equals the cluster's GPU-seconds. Quota changes can be made mid-{{period}}, and occasionally backdated. The fair-share priority shown in a report must equal what the scheduler used at that moment. Chargeback for a closed {{period}} must not change silently.
sections.assumptions: All sizes, rates and policies are hypothetical. The scheduler emits an event for every submit, start, preemption, checkpoint and end, with GPUs or slices held. GPU models differ in capability; how to weight them is your call.
sections.criteria: An append-only interval ledger from scheduler events as the source of truth; demand-aware definitions of promised, delivered, borrowed, lent and lost, stated precisely; hourly reconciliation against capacity including unavailable GPUs; slice and model weighting made explicit and agreed; decayed usage computed incrementally with snapshots so past priorities reproduce exactly (and a shared implementation with the scheduler); closed periods frozen with corrections issued as adjustments; an explanation of waits from the queue state at the time; preemption cost measured as lost work; adapts to each incident with diagnosis, recovery and prevention.

clarifications.q: If a team had no queued work, was its guarantee "undelivered"?
clarifications.a: That is the central definitional question. Decide and defend it.

clarifications.q: Does preempted work count as delivered?
clarifications.a: The GPUs were used, but work since the last checkpoint was lost. Report it somehow; you decide how it is charged.

clarifications.q: Who borrows when several teams want idle GPUs?
clarifications.a: The team with the best fair-share priority, then by submission time.

clarifications.q: Is decayed usage counted per team or per user?
clarifications.a: Per team for this exercise; per-user fairness inside a team is out of scope.

hints: Make the ledger the source of truth: intervals of (job, team, GPUs or slices, start, end, reason ended), from which every report is a projection.
"Delivered" only means something against demand: a guarantee is unmet only while the team had work waiting that could have used it.
Decayed usage can be updated incrementally (decay the old value by the elapsed time, add the new usage); store snapshots so any past value can be reproduced exactly.
followups: Define promised, delivered, borrowed, lent and lost precisely, then compute them for one team over one day from a few example events.
How do you make the fair-share priority in your reports equal the scheduler's at any moment, including after a scheduler restart?
A quota grant is backdated to the start of the {{period}}. What changes in the reports, the chargeback and the priorities that were already used?
A team asks why their job waited six hours yesterday. What does your explanation show them?
Leadership wants to know whether lending idle GPUs is worth the preemptions it causes. What would you measure?

rules.ask: A team's GPUs were allocated all day but their jobs used them at 30%. Is that delivered? Whose problem is it?
Two hours of a borrowed job's work were lost because it could not checkpoint in the grace period. Who pays for those GPU-hours in your chargeback?
The scheduler and your report both compute decay in floating point. How do you make them agree to the last digit a month later?
Recomputing a month of decayed usage after a correction takes how long, and which already-sent reports change?
A slice holds a small fixed share of a GPU's memory but is worth more than that share to some jobs. How do you weight it, and who agrees to that?

incidents: A team says it received 60% of its guarantee last {{period}}; the report says 100%. The report counted every GPU-hour on the team's quota, including jobs preempted hours after their last checkpoint and GPUs held by jobs that were waiting on input data.
The scheduler restarts and rebuilds decayed usage from zero. For about a day, the team that had used the most gets the best priority, and other teams' jobs wait behind it.
A quota correction is backdated to the start of the {{period}}, and last {{period}}'s chargeback invoices change without notice to the teams that already reported them to finance.

An owner team submits a large job and dozens of borrowed jobs are preempted at once. Half of them cannot write a checkpoint within the grace period because the shared storage is saturated by everyone checkpointing together.

templates.title: Profiler trace analytics: kernel-level summaries and run-to-run comparison
templates.subtopic: large trace ingestion, normalisation, comparison

sections.scenario: Teams running training and inference jobs on GPUs capture profiler traces: for a window of steps on chosen ranks, a timeline of kernels executed on each GPU (several streams can run at once), memory copies, CPU-side API calls that launched them, collective operations, and ranges the code annotates such as "forward", "layer 12" or "optimizer". About {{traces_per_day}} traces arrive per day, each around {{trace_size}} compressed, in formats that change with the profiler's version. Engineers want, for any trace, time per kernel and per annotated range, GPU idle gaps and the overlap of compute with communication; and for two runs of the same model, before and after a library or driver upgrade, an answer to "what got slower, and by how much?"
sections.problem: Design the trace analytics platform: upload, parsing into a common event model, storage, per-trace summaries, search across traces ("which jobs spend more than a fifth of their step in this kernel?") and run-to-run comparison. Say how you avoid double counting when kernels overlap, how kernel names are normalised, and how you keep comparisons fair when the two runs differ in batch size or in the number of steps captured.
sections.constraints: A summary for a trace should be ready within 10 minutes of upload. Raw traces are kept {{retention}}; summaries for longer. Traces belong to teams and may reveal model names and file paths, so access follows the team that owns the job. Kernel names are long, generated from templates, and change across library versions.
sections.assumptions: All sizes and rates are hypothetical. Each trace arrives with its job id, rank, the software stack versions and the step range captured. Event timestamps are on one clock per trace, after the profiler aligns CPU and GPU timelines.
sections.criteria: Asynchronous, chunked ingestion with per-team fairness and back-pressure; one versioned parser per profiler format into a common columnar event model; versioned kernel-name normalisation (families, mapping tables across library versions); interval-union busy time, exclusive time and exposed communication defined precisely; summaries per step and range with warm-up and checkpoint steps marked; comparisons aligned on step and range, normalised by work, with variance shown; partitioned and clustered storage plus precomputed aggregates for cross-trace search; access by owning team; schema checks that catch unit changes; adapts to each incident with diagnosis, recovery and prevention.

clarifications.q: Are traces from all ranks of a job?
clarifications.a: Usually a few ranks; sometimes every rank of a job for a few steps, which arrives as hundreds of files at once.

clarifications.q: Should warm-up steps be included?
clarifications.a: The first steps after start or after a checkpoint restore are slower; you decide how they are treated.

clarifications.q: What is "time" for a kernel that overlaps another?
clarifications.a: That is for you to define; the answer differs for "where does the GPU spend time?" and "what is on the critical path?".

clarifications.q: Are the two runs in a comparison always the same configuration?
clarifications.a: Same model, but batch size, sequence length or the number of GPUs can differ. The user says which run is the baseline.

hints: Parse once into a columnar event table (trace, rank, stream, kind, name, normalised name, start, end, range path) and build every summary from it.
Summing kernel durations overstates busy time when streams overlap; compute the union of busy intervals per GPU, and separately the time each kernel is the only thing running.
Compare runs per step and per annotated range first, then drill into kernels inside the range that changed; normalise by work done (tokens or samples) when batch sizes differ.
followups: Walk through what happens when every rank of a 512-rank job uploads its trace at once, from arrival to a ready summary.
Define "GPU busy time", "kernel time" and "exposed communication time" for a step where compute and an all-reduce overlap.
A library upgrade renames and splits a kernel. How does your comparison still say which work got slower?
How would you answer the cross-trace search query quickly over {{retention}} of traces?
How do you show a comparison's uncertainty, so a 3% difference between two single runs is not reported as a regression?

rules.ask: Two streams each run kernels for 8 ms of a 10 ms step, overlapping by 6 ms. What does your summary say the GPU was busy for?
One trace holds tens of millions of events. How long does loading and summarising {{traces_per_day}} of them a day take in that database?
Which version of your normaliser produced last month's summaries, and what happens to comparisons across a normaliser change?
The baseline run has 20 captured steps and the new one has 5, one of them a checkpoint step. How does your comparison treat that?
How do you lay out the event table so "time in this kernel across all jobs last week" does not read every trace?

incidents: After a library upgrade, a comparison reports a model's attention kernels as twice as slow. The new library split one kernel into two with different names, and the old name now appears half as often.
Every rank of a 512-rank job uploads a {{trace_size}} trace in the same minute. The parser backlog grows to nine hours and every other team's summaries miss the 10-minute target.
On jobs that run compute and communication on separate streams, summed kernel time per step is 40% larger than the step's wall-clock time, and a dashboard shows GPU busy time of 140%.
A profiler update changes the unit of one event type's duration field, and a week of summaries shows a family of kernels as a thousand times faster before anyone notices.

templates.title: Power and thermal telemetry: rack caps, throttling and job slowdowns
templates.subtopic: time alignment, throttling attribution, capping policy

sections.scenario: A GPU cluster operator runs {{racks}} racks of GPU nodes. Each rack has a power cap of {{rack_cap}} set by the facility; a node can set a power limit on each GPU, and a GPU lowers its clocks when it reaches its power limit or a temperature limit. Node telemetry, every {{sample}}, gives per-GPU power draw, temperature, clock frequency and a bitmask of the reasons clocks are currently reduced (power limit, thermal limit, hardware slowdown, idle; this exercise's set). The facility's own systems report each rack's measured power once a minute and the inlet temperature at each rack. Training jobs are synchronous: when they start a step, every GPU in the job draws power at once.
sections.problem: Design the power and thermal telemetry platform: ingestion from node and facility sources, time alignment between them, rack- and row-level views, detection of throttling episodes and their reasons, the link from throttling to the jobs that ran on those GPUs and to their slowdown, and the feedback into capping policy (per-GPU limits that keep each rack under its cap with {{headroom}} margin) and capacity planning (how many more nodes a rack or row can take).
sections.constraints: A rack must not exceed its cap for more than a few seconds. Node and facility timestamps come from different clocks and different sample periods; the facility's readings are stamped at the end of each minute. Job slowdown must be stated against the job's own unthrottled step time, not against a guess. Telemetry is kept at full resolution for 30 days and as rollups for two years.
sections.assumptions: All caps, rates and limits are hypothetical, and the throttle-reason set is the exercise's own. Job step times are available from the training observability system, keyed by job, rank and step, with the node and GPU of each rank.
sections.criteria: Separate ingestion for node and facility sources with explicit window semantics and time alignment; rack and row aggregation that respects the facility's interval stamps; throttling episodes with multi-reason accounting; episodes joined to job intervals and to step times, with slowdown measured against the job's own unthrottled steps and driven by the worst GPU in a synchronous job; capping policy evaluated by controlled rollout per job type, with throughput cost measured; awareness of correlated power ramps from synchronous jobs (staggered starts, ramp limits, placement by headroom); retention with rollups; adapts to each incident with diagnosis, recovery and prevention.

clarifications.q: Who sets per-GPU power limits?
clarifications.a: Today, a fixed fleet-wide value. Part of your design may be to change that.

clarifications.q: Can more than one throttle reason be active at once?
clarifications.a: Yes; the bitmask can have several bits set. Decide how you count time per reason.

clarifications.q: Does one throttled GPU slow a whole job?
clarifications.a: In a synchronous job, usually yes: every rank waits for the slowest one at each collective.

clarifications.q: Can a job be moved to avoid a hot rack?
clarifications.a: Not while running; the scheduler can take rack power headroom into account when placing new jobs.

hints: Align sources on event time per rack: aggregate GPU power into the facility's one-minute windows, with each window's start and end made explicit, before comparing them.
Turn the bitmask into episodes (start, end, reasons) per GPU, then join episodes to the job intervals that held each GPU.
For a synchronous job, the slowdown follows the worst GPU in the job, not the average; compare its step times inside and outside episodes.
followups: Estimate the telemetry volume per day at {{sample}} sampling and say what you keep at full resolution.
Walk through how you show that a 25% slowdown of one job last night was caused by thermal throttling on 6 of its GPUs.
How do you choose per-GPU power limits so each rack stays under {{rack_cap}} with {{headroom}} margin, and how do you measure what that costs in throughput?
A large job starts and every GPU in three racks ramps from idle to full power within a second. What does your platform see, and what should the policy do?
Facilities wants to add nodes to a row. What evidence does your platform give them, and how confident is it?

rules.ask: Forty nodes in one row throttle while the rest of the cluster is fine. What does your cluster-average clock show, and what do the jobs on those nodes experience?
The facility stamps each one-minute reading at the end of the minute and your GPU samples are stamped at the start of each {{sample}} interval. Show me the join.
Lowering every GPU's limit keeps racks under the cap but slows some jobs and not others. How do you find out which, before you roll it out everywhere?
A rack is above its cap for four seconds. Who or what acts first, and in what time?
The bitmask shows both the power-limit and thermal bits for ten minutes. Which cause do you report, and why?

incidents: A large synchronous job starts on three racks. Every GPU ramps from idle to full power within a second and each rack briefly exceeds {{rack_cap}}; the facility raises an alarm, and the next time the job restarts after a failure it happens again.

A cooling unit fails in one row. Forty nodes throttle for thermal reasons, and jobs spanning those nodes and healthy ones slow by 25%, while the cluster-wide average clock frequency on the dashboard falls by only 2%.

A join of facility rack power with the sum of GPU power shows racks apparently drawing less power than their own GPUs for several hours a day. The facility's readings are stamped at the end of each minute and the join treats them as the start.

The fleet-wide per-GPU power limit is lowered so that racks keep {{headroom}} headroom. Some jobs slow by 12%, others not at all, and leadership asks whether the change was worth it and for which jobs.

templates.title: Two teams with hard deadlines and not enough GPUs for both
templates.subtopic: allocation decisions, decision rights, transparent trade-offs

need_a: a model release promised to customers
a training run that must finish before a product launch
need_b: a benchmark submission with a fixed external date
a large evaluation that gates a partner's integration

sections.scenario: You lead the platform team that runs a shared GPU cluster. For the next {{weeks}} weeks two teams each need most of it: one for {{need_a}}, the other for {{need_b}}. Their combined requests exceed the cluster's capacity by {{shortfall}}. Both deadlines are real, both teams' leaders say theirs comes first, and each has asked you, separately, to guarantee their share. New capacity cannot arrive within {{weeks}} weeks. You have been asked to propose an allocation and explain it.
sections.problem: What do you do? Cover what you check about the requests themselves, which options reduce the shortfall before anyone has to lose, who should make the priority call and how you prepare it for them, how the allocation is written down and enforced, how you tell both teams, and what you watch and revisit over the {{weeks}} weeks. Then tell me about a real time you had to divide a scarce resource between people who all needed it, with what happened, or say that you have not and reason it through.
sections.constraints: You own the cluster and its data; you do not own the business priority between the two teams. Every other team on the cluster also has work. Whatever you decide will be read as a precedent.
sections.assumptions: The situation, teams and figures are hypothetical.
sections.criteria: Verifies the requests against history and asks how they were estimated; reduces the gap before allocating (efficiency work with measured gains, preemptible scheduling, pausing other work with its cost stated, outside capacity); separates the platform's decisions from the business priority and prepares a clear, fair decision for the person who owns it, with options and consequences; writes the allocation down and enforces it in the scheduler; communicates to both teams together and to the rest of the cluster; tracks progress and has a rule for re-balancing; real example with what happened and personal contribution, or honestly hypothetical.

clarifications.q: Are the requests accurate?
clarifications.a: They are each team's estimate. Neither has shown you how it was made.

clarifications.q: How efficiently do the teams use GPUs today?
clarifications.a: Your telemetry shows one team's jobs average 45% utilisation of the GPUs they hold; the other's about 70%.

clarifications.q: Who is above both teams?
clarifications.a: A director who would rather not decide, but will if asked clearly.

clarifications.q: Can the other teams on the cluster give anything up?
clarifications.a: Some of their work could pause for a few weeks, at a cost they will want to know about.

hints: Before anyone loses, test the numbers: how was each request estimated, and what does the team's history say about it?
Shrink the gap first: efficiency fixes, scheduling (preemptible and off-peak work), pausing lower-priority work, and borrowing capacity from elsewhere.
Your job is to make the trade-off visible and the decision clean, not to choose the business priority yourself.
followups: How would you check each team's request, and what would you do if one is clearly inflated?
What options shrink the shortfall, and roughly how much could each give?
What do you put in front of the director, and how do you make sure both teams think it is fair?
Two weeks in, one team is ahead of plan and the other behind. Do you move GPUs? Who decides?
In your real example, how did the team that got less react, and what did you do about it?

rules.ask: An even split makes both teams miss. Is that better or worse than one team making it for sure?
What exactly do you ask the director to decide, and what do you decide yourself?
The 45% team says their utilisation is low because of input data stalls they cannot fix in time. What do you do with that?
Your priority scheme preempts the other teams' jobs. Who tells them, and what do they get in return?
Which part of the decision did you make personally, and how did you explain it?

templates.title: Benchmark results the team cannot reproduce a month later
templates.subtopic: reproducibility, correcting a published result, changing practice

audience: a performance report sent to customers
a decision to standardise every team on a new library version
a public write-up on the team's blog
result: training throughput in samples per second
time to train to a target accuracy
inference requests per second at a latency target

sections.scenario: A month ago your team published a benchmark of {{result}} for a model on a GPU cluster, and it was used in {{audience}}. An engineer rerunning it this week, with what they believe is the same setup, gets a result {{gap}} worse. Nobody kept a full record of the original environment: the driver, toolkit and library versions, the container, firmware, power and clock settings, which nodes were used, and the exact configuration are partly in a notebook and partly in people's memories. One engineer suggests quietly rerunning until a number close to the original appears.
sections.problem: What do you do in the first day, the first week and afterwards? Cover how you find out which number is right, how you decide whether and how to correct the published result and who needs to know, how you respond to the suggestion to rerun until it matches, and what you change so the team's benchmarks are reproducible from now on. Then tell me about a real time a result you or your team reported turned out to be wrong or irreproducible, with what happened, or say that you have not and reason it through.
sections.constraints: The original engineer is still on the team. The people who used the result are expecting a follow-up soon. Reruns cost scarce cluster time.
sections.assumptions: The situation and figures are hypothetical.
sections.criteria: Refuses to rerun until it matches and says why; establishes run-to-run variance and reconstructs the original environment, then isolates the cause one factor at a time; distinguishes "the original was an outlier" from "something changed" and acts differently on each; corrects the published result promptly, proportionately and to everyone who used it, owning the sign-off; treats the original engineer fairly (a process failure, not a person); changes practice so every benchmark records its full environment (software, firmware, power and clock settings, nodes, configuration) and reports multiple runs with spread; real example with what happened and personal contribution, or honestly hypothetical.

clarifications.q: Was the original run a single run?
clarifications.a: Three runs; the best was reported.

clarifications.q: Has anything changed on the cluster since?
clarifications.a: A driver update, a firmware update on some nodes, and a change to the default per-GPU power limit, all in the last month.

clarifications.q: Is the difference within normal run-to-run variation?
clarifications.a: Nobody knows; variance was never measured.

clarifications.q: Who owns the published result?
clarifications.a: Your team, and you signed off on it.

hints: Treat it as a bisection: recover as much of the original environment as you can, reproduce either number, then change one factor at a time.
Measure run-to-run variance before arguing about a {{gap}} difference.
Decide on the correction from the evidence and the audience's use of the number, not from how it looks.
followups: Which factors would you test first, and why those?
You find the original was the best of three runs on a few unusually fast nodes. How do you correct it, and to whom?
How do you handle the suggestion to rerun until the number matches, and the engineer who made it?
What does a reproducible benchmark record contain, and how do you make the team actually use it?
In your real example, what did the correction cost you, and what did it earn?

rules.ask: How many runs do you need before you trust the difference, and how much cluster time is that?
The correction will embarrass a manager who quoted the number widely. Does that change what you publish or when?
Pinning software versions does not pin firmware, power limits or which nodes you get. What else do you record?
The variance turns out to be 6%. What should the original report have said?
How do you talk to the engineer who ran the original benchmark?

templates.title: Working with a hardware team whose release cycle is measured in years
templates.subtopic: different cadences, requirements, long-horizon planning

you_own: the telemetry pipeline that collects counters from every GPU in a cluster
the scheduler that places jobs on GPUs
a software library that applications use to run on the hardware
ask: a new hardware counter that would expose a class of failures you can only guess at today
a change in how the hardware reports why it reduced its clocks
a way to read telemetry without interrupting running work

sections.scenario: Your team owns {{you_own}} and ships every week. You depend on a hardware team whose generation takes about {{cycle}} from design freeze to systems in the field. You need {{ask}}; without it, your team keeps building workarounds that are expensive and still miss things. The next generation's design freezes in {{freeze_months}} months; after that, changes are close to impossible. The hardware team has hundreds of requests, finite silicon area, power and validation time, and has never heard of your team.
sections.problem: How do you get your request properly considered? Cover how you learn their constraints and decision process, how you make the case in terms they can weigh, what you ask for (and what smaller or different asks could serve), what your team does in the {{cycle}} before anything ships, and how you build a working relationship that lasts beyond this one request. Then tell me about a real time you depended on a team that worked on a very different cadence or with very different constraints, with what happened, or say that you have not and reason it through.
sections.constraints: You cannot escalate your way into their design. Your team's workarounds must keep running for at least {{cycle}} whatever the answer.
sections.assumptions: The situation, teams and timelines are hypothetical.
sections.criteria: Learns the hardware team's process, constraints and timelines before asking; states the need separately from a proposed mechanism; quantifies the cost of not having it from incident and effort data and gathers other teams with the same need; makes the request early, concise and in their terms, with priorities and smaller alternatives; plans for the {{cycle}} gap with software or firmware measures and keeps workarounds maintained; builds a lasting relationship (field data shared back, early feedback on their designs, a named contact); accepts a "no" with a plan; real example with what happened and personal contribution, or honestly hypothetical.

clarifications.q: Does the hardware team take requests from software teams?
clarifications.a: Yes, through a requirements process with a review each quarter.

clarifications.q: Do you have data on what the missing capability costs?
clarifications.a: Incident records and your team's time on workarounds, not yet summarised.

clarifications.q: Could the capability be delivered without new hardware?
clarifications.a: Possibly, partly, through firmware or the driver; you do not know yet.

clarifications.q: Who else wants it?
clarifications.a: You suspect other teams do, but nobody has asked them.

hints: Learn how they decide before you ask: the cost to them of a feature, who weighs requests and when.
Quantify the cost of not having it with your own data, and find other teams who would benefit.
Separate the need from your proposed solution; they may know a cheaper way to meet the need.
followups: What does your written request contain, and how long is it?
They reply that the counter costs area and validation time they do not have this generation. What do you do?
What could firmware or software deliver in the meantime, and how would you find out?
How do you keep the relationship useful for the next request, and the one after?
In your real example, what did you learn about the other team's constraints that changed your ask?

rules.ask: You escalate and the request is added. What has it cost you with the hardware team for the next {{cycle}}?
What single number from your data would make the hardware team's reviewer take it seriously, and how sure are you of it?
Your workaround is good enough for most cases. Do you still push for the hardware change, and how do you decide?
Three other teams want something similar but slightly different. Do you merge the asks, and who owns the merged request?
What did you personally write, present or negotiate?

templates.title: Admitting that a design you championed was the wrong call
templates.subtopic: reversing your own decision, sunk cost, decision practice

design: a custom checkpoint format for training jobs, instead of the widely used one
a central job-telemetry database for every cluster, instead of keeping telemetry in each cluster
an in-house job launcher wrapped around the cluster scheduler
signal: it costs about three times what you estimated
most of the teams it was built for have built workarounds rather than use it
it has been involved in two of the last five incidents

sections.scenario: {{months}} months ago you argued hard for {{design}}. Others proposed a simpler path; your argument won, and you led the build. Now {{signal}}. You have looked at the evidence, and you believe the original decision, not just its execution, was wrong. Several engineers spent most of that time building it, and some of them still believe in it. Your manager backed you at the time.
sections.problem: What do you do? Cover how you make sure it is the decision and not the execution or bad luck, how and to whom you say so, what you propose (move away, fix, or keep it with limits), how you handle the engineers who built it and the people who argued for the other path, and what you change in how you and the team make such decisions. Then tell me about a real time you reversed a decision you had championed, with what happened, or say that you have not and reason it through.
sections.constraints: Teams depend on the current design today, so any change must be gradual. Your credibility is part of what is at stake, and so is the team's trust in future proposals.
sections.assumptions: The situation and figures are hypothetical.
sections.criteria: Tests the decision against its own assumptions and separates decision quality from execution and luck; raises it early, plainly and first with the people who must act, with evidence and a proposal; owns the original call, including credit to whoever raised the concern; decides the next step on future costs and benefits with a gradual, safe migration or a fix with kill criteria; treats the builders with respect and keeps their work's value visible; changes decision practice (written assumptions, review dates, exit criteria); real example with what happened and personal contribution, or honestly hypothetical.

clarifications.q: Did anyone predict this?
clarifications.a: One engineer raised the cost concern in the original review, and you argued them down.

clarifications.q: Is there a cheap way out?
clarifications.a: Moving to the simpler path would take about a quarter of one team's time.

clarifications.q: Does your manager know?
clarifications.a: They know about the symptom, not your conclusion.

clarifications.q: Could it be fixed instead?
clarifications.a: Partly; you estimate a fix costs more than moving away and leaves the main weakness.

hints: Write down the assumptions the original decision rested on, and check which ones failed.
Say it plainly and first to the people who need to act on it, with the evidence and a proposal; do not wait to be found out.
Judge the next step by future cost and benefit only; what was spent is gone either way.
followups: How do you tell the decision was wrong rather than badly executed?
What exactly do you say to your manager, and to the engineer who raised the concern originally?
The engineers who built it want to fix it instead. How do you decide, and how do you keep them motivated either way?
What would you change in how the team makes decisions like this one?
In your real example, what did reversing the decision cost you, and what did it gain?

rules.ask: The engineers who built it hear "sunk cost" as "your year was wasted". How do you talk about it with them?
What evidence would show the fix is working, and by when would you give up on it?
Your next proposal is next quarter. What will people remember about this one, and what do you want them to remember?
What decision-making practice changes because of it, concretely, and who checks it is followed?
You championed it. Which parts of the decision were yours alone?

templates.title: Project deep dive, re-examined for accelerated computing at cluster scale
templates.subtopic: design decisions, failures, scaling onto GPU clusters

angle: the bottleneck that was hardest to find
the decision that most changed what the system cost
the failure that taught you the most
cluster_feature: jobs that span thousands of GPUs and all stop when one node fails
GPUs shared between jobs by partitioning each into fixed-size slices
a power cap per rack that the system must stay under

sections.scenario: In this part of the loop you describe a system you designed or substantially changed, one that other teams or customers depended on. The interviewer will go deep on {{angle}}, then ask how the system would have to change if it ran on, or served, a large GPU cluster at {{scale}} today's load, where work is expensive per hour, tightly synchronised across many machines, and subject to {{cluster_feature}}.
sections.problem: Give a five-minute overview: the problem, the users, the scale in numbers, the architecture and your role. Then go deep on {{angle}}. Then reason through what changes at {{scale}} the load on a GPU cluster with {{cluster_feature}}. If you have never worked with GPUs or accelerated computing, say so, pick the closest system you have worked on, and be clear which parts you are recalling and which you are reasoning through.
sections.constraints: Your own project only. Describe it without revealing anything a previous employer would not want shared; round numbers are fine if you say so.
sections.assumptions: The GPU cluster setting is hypothetical.
sections.criteria: Clear problem framing with real numbers (volume, peak and average, latency or throughput targets, cost); depth on the chosen angle down to data paths, bottlenecks and failure modes; decisions explained with alternatives and evidence; an honest account of what broke and what changed; a scaling analysis that names the first bottleneck and how it would be seen early; a concrete reasoning about the GPU-cluster feature (checkpoint interval against failure rate, slice sizing and isolation, power headroom and its throughput cost) with its new failure modes; own contribution separated from the team's, or an honest statement of reasoning rather than recall.

clarifications.q: Does it have to involve GPUs?
clarifications.a: No. Any system that moves, stores or computes data others depend on counts; the GPU part is reasoning.

clarifications.q: Can it be a team project?
clarifications.a: Yes, but separate what you did from what the team did.

clarifications.q: How deep should I go?
clarifications.a: Down to data paths, bottlenecks, failure modes, costs and numbers.

clarifications.q: What is special about a GPU cluster for this question?
clarifications.a: Expensive hardware that should not sit idle, work synchronised across many machines, and failures that stop a whole job. Reason from those.

hints: Lead with the problem and the numbers, including peak against average, before the architecture.
Know where the time goes in your system: compute, waiting on data, waiting on other machines, or recovering from failure.
For the GPU question, ask what keeps expensive hardware busy and what happens to a synchronised job when one part is slow or fails.
